children.title: Primal Logarithmic-Barrier Viewpoint
children.top_down_role: Primal-side barrier subproblems and their trajectory interpretation.

assumptions_latex: For each \(\mu>0\), the displayed barrier problem attains a unique minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x(\mu)\) traces the primal logarithmic-barrier path, and every associated multiplier pair \((y(\mu),s(\mu))\) satisfies primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and \(X(\mu)s(\mu)=\mu e\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard-form primal minimization with a logarithmic barrier on nonnegativity.

source_refs.locator: 5.3 The primal logarithmic barrier function p. 90
source_refs.source_title: Interior Point Methods for Linear Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(\mu>0\), define
\[
x(\mu)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{Ax=b,\,x>0}\left\{c^{\mathsf T}x-\mu\sum_{i=1}^n\log x_i\right\}.
\]
The first-order optimality conditions assert that there exist \(y(\mu)\in\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(s(\mu)\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that
\[
Ax(\mu)=b,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}y(\mu)+s(\mu)=c,\qquad X(\mu)s(\mu)=\mu e,
\]
with \(x(\mu)>0\) and \(s(\mu)>0\). Thus the barrier minimizers form the primal projection of the primal-dual central path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal barrier minimizers, indexed by a positive barrier parameter, form the primal projection of the central path and satisfy perturbed complementarity with suitable dual variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal Logarithmic-Barrier Viewpoint

source_witnesses.locator: 5.3 The primal logarithmic barrier function p. 90
source_witnesses.source_title: Interior Point Methods for Linear Optimization

assumptions_latex: The primal barrier minimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The restriction of \(f_\mu\) to the feasible affine set is strictly convex, so its attained minimizer is unique.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict curvature of the primal logarithmic barrier on feasible directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[ f_\mu(x)=c^{\mathsf T}x-\mu\sum_{i=1}^n\log x_i,\qquad x>0, \] one has \(\nabla^2 f_\mu(x)=\mu X^{-2}\succ0\). In particular, every nonzero feasible direction \(h\in\ker A\) satisfies \[ h^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2f_\mu(x)h=\mu\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{h_i^2}{x_i^2}>0. \] Thus the restriction of \(f_\mu\) to the feasible affine set is strictly convex, and any attained primal barrier minimizer is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal log-barrier Hessian is μX⁻² and is positive on every nonzero feasible direction, making any attained minimizer unique.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal Barrier Curvature and Uniqueness

children.title: Dual Logarithmic-Barrier Viewpoint
children.top_down_role: Dual-side barrier subproblems and their trajectory interpretation.

assumptions_latex: The set \(\{(y,s):A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s>0\}\) is nonempty.
For each \(\mu>0\), the displayed barrier problem has an optimizer with a uniquely determined slack vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The dual slack trajectory \(s(\mu)\) is the dual projection of the central path and obeys \(X(\mu)s(\mu)=\mu e\) for a positive primal vector \(x(\mu)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard-form dual maximization with a logarithmic barrier on dual slacks.

source_refs.locator: 5.9 Dual logarithmic barrier function p. 105

source_refs.locator: 6 The Dual Logarithmic Barrier Method p. 107
source_refs.source_title: Interior Point Methods for Linear Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(\mu>0\), define
\[
(y(\mu),s(\mu))\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\,s>0}\left\{b^{\mathsf T}y+\mu\sum_{i=1}^n\log s_i\right\}.
\]
The first-order conditions yield a vector \(x(\mu)=\mu S(\mu)^{-1}e>0\) satisfying
\[
Ax(\mu)=b,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}y(\mu)+s(\mu)=c,
\qquad X(\mu)s(\mu)=\mu e.
\]
Consequently, the dual barrier optimizers form the dual projection of the same primal-dual central path generated by the primal logarithmic barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual logarithmic-barrier optimizers generate positive slacks whose associated primal variables satisfy feasibility and perturbed complementarity, giving the dual projection of the central path.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Logarithmic-Barrier Viewpoint

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full row rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla^2\phi_\mu(y)=\mu A S(y)^{-2}A^{\mathsf T}\succ0\), so any attained dual barrier minimizer and its slack are unique.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Curvature and uniqueness of the dual logarithmic-barrier objective in dual equality coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With \(s(y)=c-A^{\mathsf T}y>0\), write the negative dual barrier objective as \[ \phi_\mu(y)=-b^{\mathsf T}y-\mu\sum_{i=1}^n\log s_i(y). \] Its Hessian is \[ \nabla^2\phi_\mu(y)=\mu A S(y)^{-2}A^{\mathsf T}. \] If \(A\) has full row rank, this matrix is positive definite throughout the dual interior. Therefore \(\phi_\mu\) is strictly convex, and any attained dual barrier optimum has a unique multiplier \(y(\mu)\) and slack \(s(\mu)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The negative dual log-barrier has Hessian μAS⁻²Aᵀ; full row rank makes it strictly convex and makes any attained optimizer unique.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Barrier Curvature and Uniqueness

children.title: Symmetric Primal-Dual Barrier Viewpoint
children.top_down_role: Coupled primal-dual organization of feasibility and complementarity.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric Primal-Dual Barrier Viewpoint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric standard-form organization of the logarithmic-barrier optimality equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The symmetric primal-dual barrier system is
\[
Ax=b,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\qquad Xs=\mu e,
\qquad x>0,\quad s>0.
\]
It treats primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and perturbed componentwise complementarity as one coupled system. Every solution satisfies
\[
c^{\mathsf T}x-b^{\mathsf T}y=x^{\mathsf T}s=n\mu.
\]
Thus \(\mu\) is both average complementarity and the duality gap divided by \(n\), and these quantities converge to zero as \(\mu\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The symmetric viewpoint couples primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and perturbed complementarity. Its barrier parameter equals both average complementarity and the duality gap divided by dimension.
assumptions_latex: The primal-dual pair is \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\) and \(\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\geq0\}\).
Both primal and dual systems have strictly feasible points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The symmetric barrier equations treat primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and componentwise complementarity as one coupled system and imply duality gap \(c^{\mathsf T}x-b^{\mathsf T}y=n\mu\).

children.title: Primal-Dual Central-Path System
children.top_down_role: The canonical coupled representation of the LP central path.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Dual Central-Path System
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical standard-form LP central path under strict primal-dual feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(\mu>0\), the primal-dual central-path point is the solution \((x(\mu),y(\mu),s(\mu))\) of
\[
Ax(\mu)=b,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}y(\mu)+s(\mu)=c,
\qquad X(\mu)s(\mu)=\mu e,
\qquad x(\mu)>0,\quad s(\mu)>0.
\]
Equivalently, every component satisfies \(x_i(\mu)s_i(\mu)=\mu\). The strict-feasibility and rank assumptions make the barrier minimizer and its associated primal-dual variables well posed. Each point also satisfies
\[
x(\mu)^{\mathsf T}s(\mu)=n\mu,
\]
so the parameter is exactly average complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The central path consists of strictly feasible primal-dual points whose componentwise products all equal the positive parameter; average complementarity is therefore exactly that parameter.
assumptions_latex: There exist \(x>0\) with \(Ax=b\) and \((y,s)\) with \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), \(s>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed equations define the canonical primal-dual central-path point \((x(\mu),y(\mu),s(\mu))\), with \(x(\mu)^{\mathsf T}s(\mu)=n\mu\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-dimensional complementarity-product representation of the central path
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric representation of the LP primal-dual central path for two complementarity pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For $n=2$, introduce product coordinates
\[
(p_1,p_2)=(x_1s_1,x_2s_2).
\]
On the primal-dual central path,
\[
p_1=p_2=\mu>0,
\]
so its image is the $45^\circ$ ray from the origin. If a point at the origin also satisfies the primal-feasibility, dual-feasibility, and nonnegativity conditions, then it is a primal-dual solution. Although $z^k(\alpha)=z^k+\alpha\Delta z^k$ is affine in the original variables, its product-coordinate image is generally curved because
\[
x_i^k(\alpha)s_i^k(\alpha)=(x_i^k+\alpha\Delta x_i^k)(s_i^k+\alpha\Delta s_i^k).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With two complementarity pairs, plotting x1s1 against x2s2 maps the central path to the positive 45-degree ray where the two products are equal. A point at the origin is a primal-dual solution if the remaining feasibility and nonnegativity conditions also hold. Straight trial lines in the original variables generally become curves in the product coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal C\ \text{maps to}\ \{(p_1,p_2):p_1=p_2=\mu>0\};\quad (p_1,p_2)=(0,0)\ \land\ \text{primal-dual feasibility and nonnegativity}\Longrightarrow\text{primal-dual solution}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal-dual central path for standard-form LP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perturbed KKT representation and its existence-uniqueness condition under the chapter's full-row-rank assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have full row rank. For each \(\tau>0\), a central-path point \((x_\tau,\lambda_\tau,s_\tau)\) satisfies \[Ax_\tau=b,\qquad A^T\lambda_\tau+s_\tau=c,\qquad (x_\tau)_i(s_\tau)_i=\tau\quad(i=1,\ldots,n),\qquad x_\tau>0,\quad s_\tau>0.\] The central path is \(\mathcal C=\{(x_\tau,\lambda_\tau,s_\tau):\tau>0\}\). A unique central-path point exists for every \(\tau>0\) if and only if \(\mathcal F^\circ=\{(x,\lambda,s):Ax=b,\ A^T\lambda+s=c,\ x>0,\ s>0\}\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The LP central path consists of strictly primal-dual feasible triples whose componentwise primal-slack products all equal the same positive parameter. Under the full-row-rank assumption, there is exactly one path point for every positive parameter if and only if the strictly primal-dual feasible set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal C=\{(x_\tau,\lambda_\tau,s_\tau):\tau>0,\ Ax_\tau=b,\ A^T\lambda_\tau+s_\tau=c,\ X_\tau S_\tau e=\tau e,\ x_\tau>0,\ s_\tau>0\},\qquad [\forall\tau>0\ \exists!\,(x_\tau,\lambda_\tau,s_\tau)]\iff\mathcal F^\circ\ne\varnothing.

children.title: Scaled Complementarity Coordinates
children.top_down_role: Scaled coordinates used for path proximity and direction analysis.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact centrality is equivalent to \(v=e\), while deviations of \(v\) or \(v^2\) from \(e\) provide dimensionless path-proximity coordinates.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimensionless componentwise coordinates for measuring proximity to perturbed complementarity.

source_refs.locator: Primal-Dual Methods: Development of the Fundamental Ideas p. 43

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the scaled complementarity coordinates componentwise by
\[
v_i=\sqrt{\frac{x_is_i}{\mu}},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n,
\]
or equivalently by \(v^2=\mu^{-1}Xs\), with squares interpreted componentwise. Then
\[
Xs=\mu e\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v=e.
\]
Thus quantities such as \(\lVert v-e\rVert\) or \(\lVert v^2-e\rVert\), for a specified norm, measure relative rather than absolute complementarity error. The scaling removes the magnitude of \(\mu\), permitting proximity comparisons across different points along a path-following trajectory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dividing each component product by the barrier scale yields dimensionless coordinates. They equal one exactly on the central path and quantify relative path proximity elsewhere.
knowledge_statements.title: Scaled Complementarity Coordinates

source_witnesses.locator: Primal-Dual Methods: Development of the Fundamental Ideas p. 43

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(n^{-1}\lVert v\rVert_2^2=\bar\mu/\mu\); hence \(\mu=\bar\mu\) exactly when the squared coordinates have mean one, which is weaker than \(v=e\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact aggregate normalization identity for squared scaled complementarity coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(v_i^2=x_is_i/\mu\), \[ \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n v_i^2=\frac{x^{\mathsf T}s}{n\mu}=\frac{\bar\mu}{\mu}. \] Consequently, \[ \mu=\bar\mu\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac1n\lVert v\rVert_2^2=1. \] Choosing the reference parameter as average complementarity therefore makes the squared coordinates have mean one, but it does not force the individual coordinates to equal one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The mean squared scaled coordinate equals average complementarity divided by the reference parameter; mean-one normalization does not imply exact centrality.
knowledge_statements.title: Average-Complementarity Normalization

children.title: Central-Path Parameterizations
children.top_down_role: Coordinates used to order and compare points along interior trajectories.

children.title: Barrier-Parameter Ordering
children.top_down_role: Path organization by the logarithmic-barrier parameter.

assumptions_latex: For every \(\mu>0\), \((x(\mu),y(\mu),s(\mu))\) is the central-path point.
The primal and dual optimal values are finite and attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The order \(0<\mu_1<\mu_2\) orders exact complementarity and gap scales by \(x_i(\mu_1)s_i(\mu_1)<x_i(\mu_2)s_i(\mu_2)\) and \(x(\mu_1)^{\mathsf T}s(\mu_1)<x(\mu_2)^{\mathsf T}s(\mu_2)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordering of exact central-path points by their positive perturbation parameter.

source_refs.locator: The Central Path p. 36

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Along the exact central path,
\[
x_i(\mu)s_i(\mu)=\mu\quad(i=1,\ldots,n),
\qquad x(\mu)^{\mathsf T}s(\mu)=n\mu.
\]
Therefore, if \(0<\mu_1<\mu_2\), then every componentwise complementarity product at \(\mu_1\) is smaller than its counterpart at \(\mu_2\), and
\[
x(\mu_1)^{\mathsf T}s(\mu_1)<x(\mu_2)^{\mathsf T}s(\mu_2).
\]
Hence decreasing parameter sequences impose the same strict ordering on exact componentwise complementarity and aggregate complementarity scales.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the exact central path, smaller barrier parameters mean strictly smaller component products and aggregate complementarity, so decreasing parameter sequences order the trajectory toward optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Barrier-Parameter Ordering

source_witnesses.locator: The Central Path p. 36

children.title: Complementarity-Gap Scale Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Path organization by complementarity and primal-dual gap scales.

children.title: Complementarity-Scale Ordering
children.top_down_role: Path indexing through complementarity scales.

assumptions_latex: \((x_k,y_k,s_k)\) lies on the exact central path with parameter \(\mu_k>0\).
The number of complementarity pairs is the fixed integer \(n\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ordering the sequence by \(\mu_k\) is equivalent to ordering it by every product \(x_{k,i}s_{k,i}\) and by average complementarity \(x_k^{\mathsf T}s_k/n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-path equivalence between barrier and componentwise complementarity orderings.

source_refs.locator: The Central Path p. 36

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every index \(k\), exact perturbed complementarity gives
\[
x_{k,i}s_{k,i}=\mu_k\quad(i=1,\ldots,n),
\qquad \frac{x_k^{\mathsf T}s_k}{n}=\mu_k.
\]
Consequently, for any indices \(j,k\),
\[
\mu_j\leq\mu_k
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x_{j,i}s_{j,i}\leq x_{k,i}s_{k,i}\ \text{for every }i
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\frac{x_j^{\mathsf T}s_j}{n}\leq\frac{x_k^{\mathsf T}s_k}{n}.
\]
The equivalences also hold with strict inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For exact central-path points, ordering by the barrier parameter, any component product, or average complementarity gives precisely the same ordering.
knowledge_statements.title: Complementarity-Scale Ordering

source_witnesses.locator: The Central Path p. 36

children.title: Duality-Gap Scale Ordering
children.top_down_role: Path indexing through primal-dual gap scales.

knowledge_statements.title: Duality-Gap Scale Ordering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-path ordering through the primal-dual objective gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each primal-dual feasible exact central-path point,
\[
c^{\mathsf T}x_k-b^{\mathsf T}y_k=x_k^{\mathsf T}s_k=n\mu_k.
\]
Define \(g_k=c^{\mathsf T}x_k-b^{\mathsf T}y_k\). For any indices \(j,k\),
\[
\mu_j\leq\mu_k\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad g_j\leq g_k,
\]
and the analogous equivalence holds with strict inequalities. Thus parameter order and duality-gap order coincide after multiplication by the fixed positive factor \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At feasible exact central-path points, the duality gap equals dimension times the barrier parameter, so both quantities induce the same ordering.
assumptions_latex: \((x_k,y_k,s_k)\) is primal-dual feasible and lies on the exact central path with parameter \(\mu_k>0\).
The primal and dual objectives are \(c^{\mathsf T}x\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ordering exact central-path points by \(\mu_k\) is equivalent to ordering them by the duality gaps \(c^{\mathsf T}x_k-b^{\mathsf T}y_k=n\mu_k\).

notation.meaning: primal-dual objective gap at index k

children.title: Scale-Equivalence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes connecting complementarity-based ordering with gap-based ordering.

knowledge_statements.title: Scale-Equivalence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant-factor scale equivalence in a componentwise central-path neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The componentwise bounds imply
\[
\alpha\mu\leq\frac{x^{\mathsf T}s}{n}\leq\beta\mu.
\]
Primal-dual feasibility also gives \(g=c^{\mathsf T}x-b^{\mathsf T}y=x^{\mathsf T}s\), so
\[
\alpha\mu\leq\frac{g}{n}\leq\beta\mu.
\]
Thus \(\mu\), average complementarity, and normalized duality gap are mutually comparable by constants independent of the current point. On the exact central path one may take \(\alpha=\beta=1\), and all three scales coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a componentwise central neighborhood, the barrier parameter, average complementarity, and normalized duality gap differ only by fixed constant factors; on the exact path they coincide.
assumptions_latex: For constants \(0<\alpha\leq\beta<\infty\), every component satisfies \(\alpha\mu\leq x_is_i\leq\beta\mu\).
The number of complementarity pairs is \(n\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Within this neighborhood, the parameter, average complementarity, and duality-gap-per-coordinate scales are equivalent up to the fixed factors \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\).

source_refs.locator: Primal-Dual Methods: Development of the Fundamental Ideas p. 43

source_witnesses.locator: Primal-Dual Methods: Development of the Fundamental Ideas p. 43

assumptions_latex: A family of points has \(n\geq 1\), \(x>0\), \(s>0\), and a reference value \(\mu>0\) at each member.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniform equivalence \(\bar\mu=\Theta(\mu)\) holds exactly when uniform two-sided aggregate bounds hold; uniform componentwise bounds are sufficient but not necessary.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact aggregate criterion and sharp boundary for constant-factor scale equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Over any family of positive points and reference scales, \(\bar\mu\) and \(\mu\) are uniformly constant-factor equivalent if and only if there are constants \(0<C_1\leq C_2<\infty\) such that \(C_1\mu\leq\bar\mu\leq C_2\mu\) throughout the family. Positivity alone gives no such comparison: with fixed \(x=s=e\), \(\bar\mu=1\) while the independent positive reference \(\mu\) can approach zero or infinity. Uniform componentwise bounds are sufficient but not necessary. For example, with \(n=2\) and products \(x_1s_1=\varepsilon\mu\), \(x_2s_2=(2-\varepsilon)\mu\), where \(0<\varepsilon<1\), one has \(\bar\mu=\mu\) for every \(\varepsilon\), although no positive componentwise lower factor remains uniform as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform aggregate bounds are the exact criterion for scale equivalence. Positivity alone is insufficient, while uniform componentwise bounds are sufficient but not necessary.
knowledge_statements.title: Aggregate Criterion and Componentwise Boundary

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Target Ordering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak monotonic ordering of primal and dual objective targets along the exact path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(p(\mu)=c^{\mathsf T}x(\mu)\) and \(d(\mu)=b^{\mathsf T}y(\mu)\). For \(0<\mu_1<\mu_2\),
\[
p(\mu_1)\leq p(\mu_2),
\qquad
d(\mu_1)\geq d(\mu_2).
\]
At every exact central-path point,
\[
p(\mu)-d(\mu)=x(\mu)^{\mathsf T}s(\mu)=n\mu.
\]
Consequently, a decreasing parameter sequence produces nonincreasing primal objective targets, nondecreasing dual objective targets, and linearly decreasing primal-dual target separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: As the barrier parameter decreases, primal objective targets improve downward, dual targets improve upward, and their separation equals dimension times the parameter.
assumptions_latex: For every \(\mu>0\), \((x(\mu),y(\mu),s(\mu))\) is an exact central-path point.
The primal and dual optimal values are finite.
The primal barrier minimizer is unique for each \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The primal target \(p(\mu)=c^{\mathsf T}x(\mu)\) is nondecreasing in \(\mu\), while the dual target \(d(\mu)=b^{\mathsf T}y(\mu)\) is nonincreasing, and \(p(\mu)-d(\mu)=n\mu\).

notation.meaning: primal objective target along the path
dual objective target along the path

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict monotonicity of each individual objective target fails in general.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharpness of weak objective ordering along the exact central path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[ \min\{0:x_1+x_2=1,\ x\geq0\}, \] the exact central path has \(x(\mu)=(1/2,1/2)\), \(s(\mu)=2\mu e\), and \(y(\mu)=-2\mu\). Thus \(p(\mu)=0\) while \(d(\mu)=-2\mu\). The primal target is constant even though the barrier parameter and duality gap vary strictly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-objective simplex has a constant primal central-path target, so individual objective-target monotonicity is generally only weak.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Objective-Target Monotonicity Need Not Be Strict

children.title: Strict-Interior Regime
children.top_down_role: The ordinary regime supporting primal-dual barrier-path construction.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Interior Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordinary full-dimensional strict-feasibility regime for standard-form primal-dual LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The standard-form primal-dual pair is in the strict-interior regime precisely when
\[
\exists x^0>0:\ Ax^0=b,
\qquad
\exists (y^0,s^0)\text{ with }s^0>0:\ A^{\mathsf T}y^0+s^0=c.
\]
In this regime, both logarithmic barriers have nonempty domains. For each \(\mu>0\), their first-order conditions can be coupled as
\[
Ax=b,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,
\qquad Xs=\mu e,
\qquad x>0,\quad s>0.
\]
If redundant equality rows are removed, the associated equality multiplier is uniquely represented.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict-interior operation requires a positive primal feasible point and a dual feasible point with positive slack, making both logarithmic barriers and the central path well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict primal-dual feasibility makes the logarithmic barriers finite on nonempty feasible domains and supports a positive central-path point for every \(\mu>0\), subject to the usual rank reduction for multiplier uniqueness.

notation.meaning: strictly feasible dual multiplier and slack

source_refs.locator: The Central Path p. 7

source_witnesses.locator: The Central Path p. 7

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full row rank after redundant equality rows are removed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The positive central equations have exactly one solution \((x(\mu),y(\mu),s(\mu))\), and its primal-dual gap is \(n\mu\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and uniqueness of each standard-form primal-dual central point in the strict-interior regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\mu>0\), the system \[Ax=b,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\qquad Xs=\mu e,\qquad x>0,\ s>0\] has a unique solution \((x(\mu),y(\mu),s(\mu))\). Its primal component is the unique minimizer of \(c^{\mathsf T}x-\mu\sum_{i=1}^n\log x_i\) over \(Ax=b,\ x>0\), and \[c^{\mathsf T}x-b^{\mathsf T}y=x^{\mathsf T}s=n\mu.\] If the original equality description is rank deficient but consistent, rank reduction preserves the unique \(x(\mu)\) and \(s(\mu)\), while equality multipliers in the unreduced description need not be unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict primal-dual feasibility gives a unique central point for every positive parameter after equality-rank reduction, and its duality gap equals n times that parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Central-Point Well-Posedness in the Strict-Interior Regime

children.title: Equality-System Rank Regimes
children.top_down_role: Full-rank and rank-deficient equality descriptions relevant to barrier paths.

knowledge_statements.title: Equality-System Rank Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of equality-row rank on multiplier uniqueness and central-system regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The linearization of the central-path equations with variables ordered as \((x,y,s)\) has coefficient matrix
\[
J=
\begin{pmatrix}
A&0&0\\
0&A^{\mathsf T}&I\\
S&0&X
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
If \(A\) has full row rank and \(X\) and \(S\) are positive diagonal matrices, then \(J\) is nonsingular and the equality multiplier is unique. If \(A\) is row-rank deficient, then \(J\) is singular and equality multipliers are nonunique along directions in \(\ker(A^{\mathsf T})\). Removing dependent equality rows restores a full-row-rank representation while preserving the primal feasible affine set and the associated \((x,s)\) path geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full row rank ensures a regular central-path system and unique equality multipliers. Redundant equality rows cause multiplier nonuniqueness and Jacobian singularity but need not alter primal-slack geometry.
assumptions_latex: The primal equality system is \(Ax=b\), and its feasible affine set is nonempty.
At the considered barrier point, \(x>0\), \(s>0\), and \(Xs=\mu e\) for some \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Full row rank of \(A\) gives a nonsingular primal-dual Newton representation; rank deficiency makes equality multipliers nonunique and the unreduced KKT Jacobian singular, without necessarily changing \((x,s)\).

notation.meaning: diagonal matrices formed from x and s
null space of the transpose equality matrix

knowledge_statements.title: Redundant-Constraint Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that logarithmic central paths generally depend on the inequality representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimizing \(x\) over \(0<x<1\). The standard representation has barrier objective \(F_1(x;\mu)=x-\mu\log x-\mu\log(1-x)\). Repeating the constraint \(x>0\) preserves the feasible set and produces \(F_2(x;\mu)=x-2\mu\log x-\mu\log(1-x)\). For every \(\mu>0\), both objectives have unique minimizers, characterized respectively by \(1-\mu/x+\mu/(1-x)=0\) and \(1-2\mu/x+\mu/(1-x)=0\), and these minimizers are distinct. Thus the two representations have different logarithmic central paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Duplicating an inequality preserves the feasible region but changes its logarithmic barrier weight and produces a different central path in this example.
assumptions_latex: The logarithmic barrier includes one term for each listed inequality, counting repetitions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Redundant inequalities can alter the central path while leaving the feasible set unchanged.

notation.meaning: Barrier objectives for the original and redundant representations

source_refs.locator: The Central Path p. 36

source_witnesses.locator: The Central Path p. 36

assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x:g_i^{\mathsf T}x<h_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\) has a nonempty logarithmic-barrier domain.
Inequality \(i\) is listed \(q_i\in\mathbb N\) times, with one logarithmic term for every listed copy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Repeating inequality rows is exactly equivalent to assigning positive-integer weights to their logarithmic-barrier terms; consequently, equality of feasible sets alone does not imply equality of central paths.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General barrier representation induced by duplicated inequality rows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If inequality \(g_i^{\mathsf T}x<h_i\) occurs \(q_i\) times, its total logarithmic-barrier contribution is \(-\mu q_i\log r_i(x)\). The repeated-row formulation therefore has barrier objective \[c^{\mathsf T}x-\mu\sum_{i=1}^m q_i\log r_i(x)\] and stationarity equation \[c+\mu\sum_{i=1}^m q_i\frac{g_i}{r_i(x)}=0\] on the feasible affine space. The repetitions preserve the feasible set but alter the barrier weights, so they provide no general invariance of central points; the immutable one-dimensional example realizes a strict change of path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeating an inequality gives its logarithmic term an integer weight, so equivalent feasible descriptions can have different central paths.
knowledge_statements.title: Repeated Inequalities as Barrier Weights

children.title: Representation-Invariant Path Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric path features preserved across equivalent equality representations.

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has full row rank and the primal-dual central path exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An invertible change of equality coordinates preserves the primal and slack central-path trajectories.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariance is restricted to invertible equality-row transformations, not arbitrary redundant inequalities.

source_refs.locator: A Primal-Dual Framework p. 8

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the standard-form pair with central equations \(Ax=b\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), \(Xs=\mu e\), and \(x,s>0\), replace \((A,b)\) by \((TA,Tb)\). If \((x(\mu),y(\mu),s(\mu))\) solves the original equations, then \((x(\mu),T^{-\mathsf T}y(\mu),s(\mu))\) solves the transformed equations, and conversely. Hence the curves traced by \(x(\mu)\) and \(s(\mu)\), including their intrinsic geometry, are unchanged; only the equality multiplier coordinates are transformed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonsingular row operations on the equality system leave the primal and slack central paths unchanged, while transforming the equality multipliers contragrediently.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Invariant Path Geometry

source_witnesses.locator: A Primal-Dual Framework p. 8

assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x:g_i^{\mathsf T}x<h_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\) has a nonempty logarithmic-barrier domain.
\(\pi\) is a permutation of the inequality indices and \(\alpha_i>0\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Permutation and positive rescaling of inequality rows preserve the primal central path; associated inequality multipliers are relabeled and inversely rescaled.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary inequality-description transformations that change the logarithmic barrier only by an additive constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Replace each inequality \(g_i^{\mathsf T}x<h_i\) by \(\alpha_i g_i^{\mathsf T}x<\alpha_i h_i\), where \(\alpha_i>0\), and optionally permute the rows. The transformed barrier term satisfies \[-\sum_{i=1}^m\log\!\bigl(\alpha_i(h_i-g_i^{\mathsf T}x)\bigr)=-\sum_{i=1}^m\log(h_i-g_i^{\mathsf T}x)-\sum_{i=1}^m\log\alpha_i.\] Thus the primal barrier minimizer is unchanged for every \(\mu>0\). In a primal-dual inequality formulation, the corresponding inequality multipliers are permuted and scaled by \(\alpha_i^{-1}\), leaving their contribution to stationarity unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Permuting inequalities or multiplying them by positive scalars changes the logarithmic barrier only by a constant and preserves the primal central path.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Invariance Under Inequality Scaling and Permutation
knowledge_statements.title: Invariance Under Inequality Scaling and Permutation

assumptions_latex: An affine parametrization \(x=x_0+Vz\) maps \(\mathbb{R}^d\) bijectively onto \(\operatorname{aff}P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A full-dimensional barrier problem in affine-hull coordinates represents the relative-interior central path of \(P\).

notation.meaning: Indices of inequalities not identically active on the polyhedron
Basis matrix for the direction space of the affine hull

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies when the feasible set has empty ambient interior but nonempty relative interior.

source_refs.locator: A Strictly Interior Point p. 29

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I=\{i:g_i^{\mathsf T}x<h_i\text{ for some }x\in P\}\). Then \(x\in\operatorname{relint}P\) exactly when \(x=x_0+Vz\) and \(g_i^{\mathsf T}(x_0+Vz)<h_i\) for every \(i\in I\); inequalities outside \(I\) are equations on \(\operatorname{aff}P\). Consequently, for a linear objective \(c^{\mathsf T}x\), the relative-interior barrier path is the image under \(x=x_0+Vz\) of the minimizers of \(c^{\mathsf T}(x_0+Vz)-\mu\sum_{i\in I}\log(h_i-g_i^{\mathsf T}(x_0+Vz))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting the problem to its affine hull and removing inequalities that are identically active yields a full-dimensional barrier formulation of the relative-interior path.
knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Reformulation

source_witnesses.locator: A Strictly Interior Point p. 29

assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty polyhedron and its barrier is formed in \(\operatorname{aff}P\) using only inequalities not identically active on \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Affine-hull restriction can restore a nonempty logarithmic-barrier domain without ensuring that the reduced barrier problem has a unique minimizer or any minimizer.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Well-posedness boundary of the relative-interior reformulation itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty relative interior is only a domain condition. For \(P=\mathbb R\) and objective \(c=0\), the reduced barrier has no logarithmic terms and every point minimizes it, so no unique central point is selected. For \(P=[0,\infty)\) and \(c=0\), the relative-interior barrier objective is \(-\mu\log x\) on \(x>0\), which is unbounded below and has no minimizer. Thus additional boundedness or dual-interiority conditions are required for central-point existence and uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Passing to the affine hull restores a relative-interior barrier domain, but it does not alone guarantee existence or uniqueness of a central point.
knowledge_statements.title: Well-Posedness Boundary After Affine-Hull Reduction

knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Face Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional standard-form primal-dual logarithmic central path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) have full row rank, and let \((x(\mu),y(\mu),s(\mu))\) be the unique solution of \(Ax=b\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), \(Xs=\mu e\), and \(x,s>0\) for \(\mu>0\). As \(\mu\downarrow0\), the path converges to an optimal primal-dual point \((x^*,y^*,s^*)\) satisfying \(x^*\in\operatorname{relint}F_P^*\) and \((y^*,s^*)\in\operatorname{relint}F_D^*\). Thus the logarithmic central path selects distinguished relative-interior points even when the optimal faces are not singletons.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under full row rank, strict feasibility, and finite optimal value, the primal-dual central path converges to distinguished relative-interior points of the primal and dual optimal faces.
assumptions_latex: The primal and dual standard-form linear programs are strictly feasible and have finite optimal values.
The primal-dual logarithmic central path is parameterized by \(\mu>0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Analytic Centers of Optimal Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Analytic centers are taken relative to the optimal faces and their positive coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) have full row rank, let \((B,N)\) be the optimal partition, and let \((x^*,y^*,s^*)\) be the limit of the primal-dual logarithmic central path. Then \(x_N^*=0\), \(s_B^*=0\), and \(x_B^*=\operatorname*{argmax}\{\sum_{i\in B}\log x_i:x\in F_P^*,\ x_B>0\}\), while \((y^*,s_N^*)=\operatorname*{argmax}\{\sum_{i\in N}\log s_i:(y,s)\in F_D^*,\ s_N>0\}\). These unique maximizers are the relative logarithmic analytic centers of the corresponding optimal faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a full-row-rank equality system, the central-path limit is the unique relative logarithmic analytic center of each optimal face in its positive coordinates.
assumptions_latex: The standard-form primal and dual programs are strictly feasible and attain a finite common optimum.
\(B\) and \(N\) are the optimal partition index sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The central-path limit is the logarithmic analytic center of each optimal face in its positive coordinates.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimal Primal–Dual Partition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard-form optimal partition defined across all primal and dual optima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal problem \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) and dual problem \(\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\ge0\}\), define \(B=\{i:x_i>0\text{ for some primal optimum }x\}\) and \(N=\{i:s_i>0\text{ for some dual optimum }(y,s)\}\). Under primal-dual optimality, \(B\cap N=\varnothing\) and \(B\cup N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The ordered pair \((B,N)\) is the optimal primal-dual partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The optimal primal-dual partition separates indices that can be positive in a primal optimum from those whose dual slack can be positive in a dual optimum.
assumptions_latex: The primal and dual standard-form linear programs have nonempty optimal solution sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sets \(B\) and \(N\) form the optimal primal-dual partition of the coordinate indices.

knowledge_statements.title: Central-Path Smoothness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smoothness on the open parameter interval \((0,\infty)\), excluding endpoint regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) have full row rank. Suppose the standard-form primal and dual problems are strictly feasible and have finite optimal value. For each \(\mu>0\), let \(z(\mu)=(x(\mu),y(\mu),s(\mu))\) be the unique solution of \(Ax=b\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), \(Xs=\mu e\), and \(x,s>0\). Then \(z:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}^{2n+m}\) is real analytic. In particular, derivatives of every finite order exist and are continuous for \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under full row rank and strict primal-dual feasibility, the standard primal-dual central path is real analytic for every positive barrier parameter.
assumptions_latex: A strictly feasible primal-dual point exists and the optimal value is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The standard primal-dual central path is real analytic for every positive barrier parameter.

notation.meaning: Diagonal matrices formed from primal variables and dual slacks

children.title: Central-Path Derivative Asymptotics
children.top_down_role: Boundedness and limiting behavior of path derivatives.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact derivatives at positive barrier parameters; no endpoint boundedness is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have full row rank and let \(z(\mu)=(x(\mu),y(\mu),s(\mu))\) satisfy \(Ax=b\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), \(XSe=\mu e\), and \(x,s>0\). For every \(\mu>0\), its derivative is the unique solution of \[Ax'=0,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}y'+s'=0,\qquad Sx'+Xs'=e.\] Consequently, \(c^{\mathsf T}x(\mu)-b^{\mathsf T}y(\mu)=n\mu\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}x'(\mu)-b^{\mathsf T}y'(\mu)=n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every positive barrier parameter, the central-path derivative is uniquely determined by the differentiated primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and complementarity equations.
assumptions_latex: \(x(\mu)>0\), \(s(\mu)>0\), and the standard primal-dual central equations hold for \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x',y',s')\) uniquely solves the differentiated central system, and the duality-gap derivative equals \(n\).
knowledge_statements.title: Central-Path Differential System

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A precise sufficient endpoint regime based on a nonsingular optimal basis; it does not characterize all degenerate limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((x^*,y^*,s^*)\) be a strictly complementary optimal limit with partition \((B,N)\). If \(|B|=m\) and \(A_B\) is nonsingular, then the central path admits a one-sided real-analytic continuation to \(\mu=0\). Hence there is a finite vector \(d\) such that \(z(\mu)=z^*+\mu d+O(\mu^2)\) and \(z'(\mu)\to d\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a strictly complementary nondegenerate optimal basis, the central path has a linear endpoint expansion and a finite limiting derivative.
assumptions_latex: The primal-dual central path converges to a strictly complementary optimum \((x^*,y^*,s^*)\).
For its optimal partition \((B,N)\), \(|B|=m\) and \(A_B\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The path extends one-sided analytically to \(\mu=0\), with \(z(\mu)=z^*+\mu d+O(\mu^2)\) and \(z'(\mu)\to d\).
knowledge_statements.title: Nondegenerate Endpoint Expansion

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Endpoint Derivative at a Strictly Complementary Nonsingular Basis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit first derivative in the sufficient nondegenerate endpoint regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the nondegenerate endpoint assumptions, let \(B=\{i:x_i^*>0\}\), \(N=\{i:s_i^*>0\}\), with \(|B|=m\) and \(A_B\) nonsingular. Writing \(X_B^*=\operatorname{Diag}(x_B^*)\) and \(S_N^*=\operatorname{Diag}(s_N^*)\), the limiting derivative is uniquely given by \[x_N'=S_N^{*-1}e,\quad x_B'=-A_B^{-1}A_NS_N^{*-1}e,\quad s_B'=X_B^{*-1}e,\] \[y'=-A_B^{-\mathsf T}X_B^{*-1}e,\quad s_N'=A_N^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-\mathsf T}X_B^{*-1}e.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a strictly complementary nonsingular optimal basis, the endpoint derivative has an explicit finite block formula.
assumptions_latex: The central path converges to a strictly complementary optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lim_{\mu\downarrow0}z'(\mu)=d\text{ with the displayed block formulas}.
review_flags: Applies to the nonsingular-basis regime, not every degenerate endpoint.
knowledge_statements.title: Endpoint Derivative at a Strictly Complementary Nonsingular Basis

assumptions_latex: The primal-dual central path converges to a strictly complementary optimum.
The limiting primal-dual KKT system is strongly regular, for example through primal and dual nondegeneracy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The central path has a first-order endpoint expansion and a finite limiting derivative with respect to \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A strong-regularity endpoint result; smoothness for positive \(\mu\) alone does not ensure bounded endpoint derivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z(\mu)=(x(\mu),y(\mu),s(\mu))\) and suppose \(z(\mu)\to z^*\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\). Under strict complementarity and strong regularity of the reduced KKT system at \(z^*\), the central equations admit a one-sided differentiable continuation to \(\mu=0\). Consequently, there exists a finite vector \(d\) such that \(z(\mu)=z^*+\mu d+o(\mu)\), and hence \(z'(\mu)\to d\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\). Without an endpoint regularity condition, analyticity on \((0,\infty)\) does not by itself imply bounded derivatives at zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With strict complementarity and a strongly regular limiting KKT system, the path has a linear endpoint expansion and its derivative converges to a finite vector.
knowledge_statements.title: Central-Path Derivative Asymptotics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The endpoint expansion is plausible under a suitable strong-regularity formulation, but no source is supplied and the exact reduced-KKT hypotheses needed for differentiable continuation are not fixed reliably.

assumptions_latex: \(D=(0,\infty)\), \(F(t)=-\log t\), and the base point is \(x=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A displacement of local norm one can reach \(\partial D\), so Dikin containment is guaranteed for strict radius below one and not for the closed unit ellipsoid in general.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharpness of the strict unit-radius condition for Dikin containment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(t)=-\log t\) on \(D=(0,\infty)\), one has \(F''(1)=1\), so the local norm at \(x=1\) is \(\lVert h\rVert_1=|h|\). The displacement \(h=-1\) has local norm one but gives \(x+h=0\notin D\). Thus the closed unit Dikin ellipsoid need not be contained in the barrier domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the one-dimensional logarithmic barrier, a displacement of local norm one reaches the boundary, so the strict unit-radius condition is sharp.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(E_x=\{x+h:\|h\|_x<1\}\). Self-concordance implies \(E_x\subset D\). Moreover, whenever \(r=\|h\|_x<1\), the Hessians satisfy \((1-r)^2H\preceq\nabla^2F(x+h)\preceq(1-r)^{-2}H\). Thus the quadratic model \(F(x)+\nabla F(x)^{\mathsf T}h+\tfrac12h^{\mathsf T}Hh\) supplies a controlled local ellipsoidal description of barrier level sets, and the associated Hessian norm changes by bounded factors inside each strict unit Dikin ellipsoid.

children.title: Scaled-Norm Centrality
children.top_down_role: Euclidean and related scaled-norm proximity families.

assumptions_latex: \((x,y,s)\) is strictly positive and satisfies the primal and dual linear equations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Scaled-norm centrality requires the normalized complementarity vector to lie in a prescribed norm ball around the all-ones vector.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean scaled complementarity neighborhood for feasible primal-dual path following.

source_refs.locator: Primal-Dual Methods: Development of the Fundamental Ideas p. 43

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the feasible standard-form primal-dual system, the Euclidean scaled-norm neighborhood is \(\mathcal N_2(\theta)=\{(x,y,s):Ax=b,\ A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ x>0,\ s>0,\ \|Xs-\mu e\|_2\le\theta\mu\}\), where \(\mu=x^{\mathsf T}s/n\). Equivalently, \(\|Xs/\mu-e\|_2\le\theta\). The exact central path is the zero-radius case \(Xs=\mu e\). Replacing the Euclidean norm by another specified norm gives the corresponding scaled-norm proximity family, with a norm-dependent neighborhood parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point is scaled-norm central when its normalized coordinatewise complementarity products are close to one in the chosen norm.
knowledge_statements.title: Scaled-Norm Centrality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension-dependent inclusions between the two standard scaled-norm neighborhoods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(r=Xs/\mu-e\), \(\|r\|_\infty\le\|r\|_2\le\sqrt n\|r\|_\infty\). Therefore \[\mathcal N_2(\theta)\subseteq\mathcal N_\infty(\theta)\subseteq\mathcal N_2(\sqrt n\,\theta).\] The factor \(\sqrt n\) is sharp for unrestricted vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two-norm centrality implies same-radius componentwise centrality, while componentwise centrality implies two-norm centrality after a sharp square-root-dimension enlargement.
assumptions_latex: The neighborhoods use the same strictly feasible primal-dual equations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal N_2(\theta)\subseteq\mathcal N_\infty(\theta)\subseteq\mathcal N_2(\sqrt n\theta).
knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean–Componentwise Neighborhood Inclusions

children.top_down_role: Coordinatewise proximity families used in wide-neighborhood analysis.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal N_{\infty}(\beta)=\{(x,y,s):\max_i|x_is_i/\mu-1|\le\beta\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual feasible, infinity-norm componentwise centrality for linear programming.

source_refs.locator: The Central Path p. 36

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a strictly positive primal-dual feasible point, define \(\mu=x^{\mathsf T}s/n\) and \(w_i=x_is_i/\mu\). Its componentwise centrality residual is \(\delta_{\infty}(x,s)=\max_{1\le i\le n}|w_i-1|\). For \(\beta\ge0\), the associated central-path neighborhood is \[\mathcal N_{\infty}(\beta)=\{(x,y,s):Ax=b,\ A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ x,s>0,\ \delta_{\infty}(x,s)\le\beta\}.\] Thus centrality is enforced separately on every complementarity product; \(\beta=0\) characterizes points satisfying \(x_is_i=\mu\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Componentwise centrality bounds every normalized complementarity product individually; radius zero gives the primal-dual central path.
knowledge_statements.title: Componentwise Centrality

children.title: Barrier-Value Centrality
children.top_down_role: Centrality measures organized through barrier-value information.

knowledge_statements.title: Barrier-Value Centrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the separable logarithmic-barrier gap of normalized complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\). For a point \((x,y,s)\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R_{++}^n\) satisfying \(Ax=b\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), set \(\mu=x^{\mathsf T}s/n\) and \(w_i=x_is_i/\mu\). Define \[h(t)=t-1-\log t,\qquad V(w)=\sum_{i=1}^n h(w_i).\] The measure satisfies \(V(w)\ge0\), with \(V(w)=0\) exactly when \(w=\mathbf1\). For \(\eta\ge0\), the barrier-value neighborhood is \[\mathcal B(\eta)=\{(x,y,s):Ax=b,\ A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ x,s>0,\ V(w)\le\eta\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Barrier-value centrality sums logarithmic barrier gaps of normalized complementarity products. It is nonnegative, vanishes exactly on the central path, and defines threshold neighborhoods.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V(w)=\sum_{i=1}^n(w_i-1-\log w_i)\ge0\), with equality exactly when \(w=\mathbf1\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coercivity of the scalar logarithmic gap bounds every coordinate on finite sublevels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h(t)=t-1-\log t\). For each finite \(\eta\ge0\), there are constants \(0<a_\eta\le1\le b_\eta<\infty\) such that \(h(t)\le\eta\) implies \(a_\eta\le t\le b_\eta\). Consequently, \[V(w)=\sum_i h(w_i)\le\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad w\in[a_\eta,b_\eta]^n.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite barrier-value sublevel bounds each normalized complementarity coordinate away from zero and infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: a_\eta\le w_i\le b_\eta\quad(i=1,\ldots,n).

notation.meaning: coordinate bounds determined by the scalar sublevel of h

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate Control by Barrier-Value Sublevels

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent representation using the unit arithmetic mean of normalized complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(w_i=x_is_i/\mu\), where \(\mu=x^{\mathsf T}s/n\), one has \(\sum_i w_i=n\). Hence \[V(w)=\sum_{i=1}^n(w_i-1-\log w_i)=-\sum_{i=1}^n\log w_i=-\log\!\left(\prod_{i=1}^n w_i\right).\] Therefore \(V(w)\le\eta\) if and only if \(\prod_iw_i\ge e^{-\eta}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Since normalized complementarity has arithmetic mean one, barrier-value centrality is the negative logarithm of the coordinate product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: V(w)=-\log\left(\prod_iw_i\right),\qquad V(w)\le\eta\iff\prod_iw_i\ge e^{-\eta}.
knowledge_statements.title: Product Representation of Barrier-Value Centrality

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Psi(w)=\sum_i\psi(w_i)\) is a centrality measure whose zero set is \(\{\mathbf1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separable proximity-function centrality on normalized complementarity products.

source_refs.locator: The Central Path p. 36

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\psi:(0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)\) have the unique minimizer \(1\), with \(\psi(1)=0\). For normalized complementarity \(w_i=x_is_i/\mu\), define \[\Psi(w)=\sum_{i=1}^n\psi(w_i).\] The proximity-function neighborhood of radius \(\tau\ge0\) is \(\mathcal P_{\psi}(\tau)=\{(x,y,s):\Psi(w)\le\tau\}\), where the points are strictly positive and primal-dual feasible. The measure is nonnegative, and \(\Psi(w)=0\) holds exactly when every \(x_is_i=\mu\), namely on the primal-dual central path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separable nonnegative kernel with unique minimum at one yields a centrality measure and threshold neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.title: Proximity-Function Centrality

children.title: Cross-Measure Comparability

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Measure Comparability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local quadratic equivalence on a positive bounded componentwise region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h(t)=t-1-\log t\) and \(V(w)=\sum_{i=1}^n h(w_i)\). If \(w\in[m,M]^n\) with \(0<m\le1\le M<\infty\), then \[\frac{1}{2M^2}\|w-\mathbf1\|_2^2\le V(w)\le\frac{1}{2m^2}\|w-\mathbf1\|_2^2.\] Thus, on this bounded positive region, barrier-value thresholds and Euclidean proximity thresholds are quantitatively comparable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a bounded positive range of component ratios, logarithmic barrier-value centrality is bounded above and below by constant multiples of squared Euclidean distance from the central path.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global One-Sided Comparison and Reverse-Bound Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalization gives a global one-sided quadratic comparison, but approach to the positive-orthant boundary prevents a global reverse comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\ge2\), \(w\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\), \(\sum_iw_i=n\), and \(V(w)=\sum_i(w_i-1-\log w_i)\). Then \[V(w)\ge\frac{1}{2n^2}\|w-\mathbf1\|_2^2.\] No finite constant \(C_n\) satisfies \(V(w)\le C_n\|w-\mathbf1\|_2^2\) for every such \(w\). Indeed, for \[w^{(\varepsilon)}=\left(\varepsilon,\frac{n-\varepsilon}{n-1},\ldots,\frac{n-\varepsilon}{n-1}\right),\] the squared norm remains bounded while \(V(w^{(\varepsilon)})\to\infty\) as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalized coordinates have a global one-sided quadratic bound, but barrier centrality diverges when a coordinate approaches zero while Euclidean distance stays bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: V(w)\ge\|w-\mathbf1\|_2^2/(2n^2),\quad\text{and no global dimension-only reverse inequality holds}.
knowledge_statements.title: Global One-Sided Comparison and Reverse-Bound Failure

children.title: Central-Path Neighborhood Families
children.top_down_role: Invariant regions distinguished by their width and acceptance role.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Euclidean and componentwise LP central-path neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions and centrality properties of two standard neighborhoods for strictly feasible primal-dual LP points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For $(x,\lambda,s)\in\mathcal F^o$, let $X=\operatorname{diag}(x)$ and $\mu=x^Ts/n$. For $\theta\in[0,1)$ and $\gamma\in(0,1]$, define
\[
\mathcal N_2(\theta)=\left\{(x,\lambda,s)\in\mathcal F^o:\|XSe-\mu e\|_2\leq\theta\mu\right\},
\]
and
\[
\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)=\left\{(x,\lambda,s)\in\mathcal F^o:x_is_i\geq\gamma\mu\ \text{for every }i=1,\ldots,n\right\}.
\]
The first condition controls the aggregate deviation of the complementarity products from their mean, while the second prevents any product from being smaller than a fixed fraction of that mean. Consequently, a sequence remaining in either neighborhood with $\mu_k\to0$ has $x_i^ks_i^k\to0$ for every $i$ while retaining strict positivity at each iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a strictly feasible primal-dual LP point, the Euclidean neighborhood bounds the collective deviations of the complementarity products from their average. The componentwise neighborhood requires every product to be at least gamma times that average. If iterates remain in either neighborhood while their average complementarity tends to zero, every complementarity product tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal N_2(\theta)=\{z\in\mathcal F^o:\|XSe-\mu e\|_2\leq\theta\mu\},\quad \mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)=\{z\in\mathcal F^o:x_is_i\geq\gamma\mu\ \forall i\};\quad z^k\in\mathcal N,\ \mu_k\to0\Longrightarrow x_i^ks_i^k\to0\ \forall i.

children.title: Narrow Central-Path Neighborhoods
children.top_down_role: Tight neighborhoods used by conservative polynomial path following.

knowledge_statements.title: Narrow Central-Path Neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard two-norm primal-dual neighborhood for feasible path following.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\). For \(0\le\theta<1\), define \[\mathcal N_2(\theta)=\{(x,y,s):Ax=b,\ A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ x,s>0,\ \|Xs-\mu\mathbf1\|_2\le\theta\mu\},\] where \(X=\operatorname{Diag}(x)\) and \(\mu=x^{\mathsf T}s/n\). Equivalently, with \(w=Xs/\mu\), membership means \(\|w-\mathbf1\|_2\le\theta\). Every member satisfies \((1-\theta)\mu\le x_is_i\le(1+\theta)\mu\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A narrow neighborhood bounds the Euclidean norm of normalized complementarity residuals by a radius below one and consequently bounds every individual complementarity product around its average.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal N_2(\theta)=\{(x,y,s):Ax=b,\ A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ x,s>0,\ \|Xs-\mu\mathbf1\|_2\le\theta\mu\}\).

source_refs.locator: Primal-Dual Methods: Development of the Fundamental Ideas p. 43

source_witnesses.locator: Primal-Dual Methods: Development of the Fundamental Ideas p. 43

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharp Coordinate Envelope in a Narrow Neighborhood
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universal sharp componentwise consequence of normalized two-norm centrality and average complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\ge2\), \(w=Xs/\mu\), and \(r=w-e\). Since \(\mu=x^{\mathsf T}s/n\), one has \(e^{\mathsf T}r=0\). Consequently, every point of \(\mathcal N_2(\theta)\) satisfies \[|w_i-1|\le \theta\sqrt{\frac{n-1}{n}},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.\] The constant is sharp as a universal consequence of \(e^{\mathsf T}r=0\) and \(\|r\|_2\le\theta\): equality is attained by one residual component \(\theta\sqrt{(n-1)/n}\) and the other components \(-\theta/\sqrt{n(n-1)}\), or with all signs reversed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Because normalized complementarity residuals sum to zero, their sharp universal coordinate deviation is θ√((n−1)/n).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e^{\mathsf T}(w-e)=0\) and \(|w_i-1|\le\theta\sqrt{(n-1)/n}\) for every \(i\).
review_flags: Sharpness is universal over normalized positive product vectors; a fixed LP may impose additional restrictions.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Coordinate Envelope in a Narrow Neighborhood

children.title: Wide Central-Path Neighborhoods
children.top_down_role: Componentwise neighborhoods permitting more aggressive progress.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)=\{(x,y,s):x_is_i\ge\gamma\mu\ \text{for every }i\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided componentwise wide neighborhood for feasible primal-dual iterates.

source_refs.locator: Primal-Dual Methods: Development of the Fundamental Ideas p. 43

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\gamma<1\), define the wide one-sided central-path neighborhood by \[\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)=\{(x,y,s):Ax=b,\ A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ x,s>0,\ x_is_i\ge\gamma\mu\ \text{for all }i\},\] where \(\mu=x^{\mathsf T}s/n\). In normalized variables \(w_i=x_is_i/\mu\), membership is \(\min_iw_i\ge\gamma\). Unlike a symmetric narrow neighborhood, this condition permits individual complementarity products to exceed \(\mu\) substantially while preventing any product from approaching zero too rapidly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A wide neighborhood imposes only a componentwise lower bound on complementarity products, allowing larger asymmetric deviations from the central path.
knowledge_statements.title: Wide Central-Path Neighborhoods

source_witnesses.locator: Primal-Dual Methods: Development of the Fundamental Ideas p. 43

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharp Product Envelope in a Wide Neighborhood
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universal dimension-dependent envelope implied by the one-sided wide-neighborhood condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(w_i=x_is_i/\mu\) for a point in \(\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)\). Because \(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i=n\) and \(w_i\ge\gamma\), every coordinate satisfies \[\gamma\le w_i\le n-(n-1)\gamma.\] Both endpoints are sharp as universal consequences of these normalized-product conditions: the upper endpoint occurs when the other \(n-1\) coordinates equal \(\gamma\). Thus fixed \(\gamma<1\) permits deviations above the mean of order \(n\), so membership does not imply a dimension-independent symmetric centrality bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A wide neighborhood bounds normalized products below by γ and universally above by n−(n−1)γ, allowing dimension-growing upper asymmetry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma\le x_is_i/\mu\le n-(n-1)\gamma\) for every \(i\).
review_flags: Sharpness is universal over normalized positive product vectors; a fixed LP may impose additional restrictions.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Product Envelope in a Wide Neighborhood

children.title: Nested Neighborhood Hierarchies
children.top_down_role: Containment structures among central-path neighborhoods.

knowledge_statements.title: Nested Neighborhood Hierarchies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite hierarchy of centrality regions ordered by set inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\in\mathbb N\) and let \(\mathcal R_1,\ldots,\mathcal R_k\) be centrality regions on the same strictly positive primal-dual feasible set. They form a nested neighborhood hierarchy when \[\mathcal R_1\subseteq\mathcal R_2\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\mathcal R_k.\] Consequently, \(z\in\mathcal R_i\) implies \(z\in\mathcal R_j\) whenever \(j\ge i\). For the standard narrow and wide neighborhoods, \[\mathcal N_2(\theta)\subseteq\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)\qquad\text{whenever}\qquad 0\le\theta<1\ \text{ and }\ 0<\gamma\le1-\theta.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nested hierarchy orders centrality regions by inclusion, so membership in a tighter region implies membership in every looser region. A standard narrow neighborhood is contained in each compatible wide neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: \(k\in\mathbb N\) and each \(\mathcal R_j\) is defined on the same strictly positive primal-dual feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z\in\mathcal R_i\) implies \(z\in\mathcal R_j\) for every \(j\ge i\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter ordering within narrow and wide central-neighborhood families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For narrow neighborhoods, \[0\le\theta_1\le\theta_2<1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathcal N_2(\theta_1)\subseteq\mathcal N_2(\theta_2).\] For one-sided wide neighborhoods, \[0<\gamma_1\le\gamma_2\le1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma_2)\subseteq\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma_1).\] Thus increasing a norm radius loosens a narrow region, whereas increasing a componentwise lower factor tightens a wide region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Narrow regions grow with their radius, while one-sided wide regions shrink as their lower-bound parameter increases.
assumptions_latex: All neighborhoods are defined on the same strictly positive primal-dual feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal N_2(\theta_1)\subseteq\mathcal N_2(\theta_2)\) and \(\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma_2)\subseteq\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma_1)\).

children.title: Switching Region Roles
children.top_down_role: Prediction, correction, and acceptance roles assigned to different regions.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal R_{\mathrm{prog}}\) and \(\mathcal R_{\mathrm{cent}}\) are centrality regions.
A progress map \(P\) and restoration map \(C\) are defined on their assigned regions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Use \(P\) while its trial point remains admissible; otherwise use \(C\) until re-entry into \(\mathcal R_{\mathrm{prog}}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract region-based switching rule; concrete algorithms choose their own thresholds and maps.

source_refs.locator: 8.6 Affine Scaling, Primal-Dual Path Following, and Predictor-Corrector Variants of Interior Point Methods p. 428

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a progress-oriented update and \(C\) a centering update. Given a progress region \(\mathcal R_{\mathrm{prog}}\) contained in an admissible region \(\mathcal R_{\mathrm{cent}}\), apply \(P\) at \(z\in\mathcal R_{\mathrm{prog}}\) only when the accepted trial point remains in \(\mathcal R_{\mathrm{cent}}\). If that test fails, switch to \(C\); continue restoration steps until an iterate re-enters \(\mathcal R_{\mathrm{prog}}\). Thus the inner region authorizes aggressive progress, while the outer region supplies the invariant required for safe restoration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inner region authorizes progress steps; approaching or leaving its admissible envelope triggers centering until the inner region is recovered.
knowledge_statements.title: Switching Region Roles

source_witnesses.locator: 8.6 Affine Scaling, Primal-Dual Path Following, and Predictor-Corrector Variants of Interior Point Methods p. 428

children.top_down_role: Permitted transitions among regions during neighborhood switching.

assumptions_latex: \(z\in\mathcal R_i\) and a trial update produces \(z^+=z+\alpha d\).
\(\mathcal R_j\) is the destination neighborhood and strict positivity is required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transition \(\mathcal R_i\to\mathcal R_j\) is admissible exactly when \(z^+\in\mathcal R_j\) and \(x^+,s^+>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic acceptance predicate for transitions between centrality regions.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a current iterate \(z=(x,y,s)\in\mathcal R_i\), direction \(d=(d_x,d_y,d_s)\), and step length \(\alpha>0\), set \(z^+=z+\alpha d\). A proposed transition from \(\mathcal R_i\) to \(\mathcal R_j\) is admissible precisely when \[Ax^+=b,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}y^++s^+=c,\qquad x^+,s^+>0,\qquad z^+\in\mathcal R_j.\] If the direction preserves the two linear feasibility equations, only positivity and the destination-neighborhood test remain to be checked.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A neighborhood transition is admissible when the trial point remains feasible and positive and satisfies the destination region's centrality test.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: LP primal-dual optimality system and centered Newton directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard-form linear programming and the Newton systems underlying positivity-preserving primal-dual interior-point directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\), with \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) of full row rank, the dual is \(\max\{b^T\lambda:A^T\lambda+s=c,\ s\geq0\}\). Primal-dual solutions are characterized by \(Ax=b\), \(A^T\lambda+s=c\), \(XSe=0\), and \((x,s)\geq0\). At a point with \(x>0\) and \(s>0\), define \(r_b=Ax-b\), \(r_c=A^T\lambda+s-c\), and \(\mu=x^Ts/n\). For \(\sigma\in[0,1]\), the centered direction solves \[\begin{bmatrix}0&A^T&I\\A&0&0\\S&0&X\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\Delta x\\\Delta\lambda\\\Delta s\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-r_c\\-r_b\\-XSe+\sigma\mu e\end{bmatrix}.\] A step length \(\alpha\in(0,1]\) is restricted so that \(x+\alpha\Delta x>0\) and \(s+\alpha\Delta s>0\). The case \(\sigma=0\) is the affine-scaling direction; positive \(\sigma\) targets positive balanced complementarity rather than zero complementarity directly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a standard-form LP with a full-row-rank constraint matrix, primal-dual optimality consists of primal and dual feasibility, nonnegativity, and componentwise complementarity. A primal-dual interior-point direction Newton-linearizes the feasibility equations and uses a centered complementarity target, while the step length preserves strict positivity. Setting the centering parameter to zero gives the affine-scaling direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{bmatrix}0&A^T&I\\A&0&0\\S&0&X\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\Delta x\\\Delta\lambda\\\Delta s\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-r_c\\-r_b\\-XSe+\sigma\mu e\end{bmatrix},\qquad x+\alpha\Delta x>0,\quad s+\alpha\Delta s>0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasible centered primal-dual Newton direction and centering tradeoff
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The sigma-parameterized Newton direction at a strictly feasible LP primal-dual point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a strictly primal-dual feasible point, \(r_b=Ax-b=0\) and \(r_c=A^T\lambda+s-c=0\). With \(x>0\), \(s>0\), \(\mu=x^Ts/n\), and \(\sigma\in[0,1]\), the direction satisfies \[\begin{bmatrix}0&A^T&I\\A&0&0\\S&0&X\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\Delta x\\\Delta\lambda\\\Delta s\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\-XSe+\sigma\mu e\end{bmatrix}.\] For \(\sigma=1\), this is the centering direction toward the central-path point whose complementarity parameter is the current \(\mu\); it primarily improves centrality and may make little progress in reducing \(\mu\). For \(\sigma=0\), it is the affine-scaling direction. Values \(0<\sigma<1\) trade reduction of \(\mu\) against improvement of centrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a strictly feasible primal-dual LP point, the feasibility residual blocks of the Newton system vanish. Sigma one gives a centering direction toward the path point with the current average complementarity, sigma zero gives affine scaling, and intermediate values trade complementarity reduction against improved centrality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{bmatrix}0&A^T&I\\A&0&0\\S&0&X\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\Delta x\\\Delta\lambda\\\Delta s\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\-XSe+\sigma\mu e\end{bmatrix},\qquad \sigma=1\text{ is centering},\quad \sigma=0\text{ is affine scaling}.

children.title: Centering Directions
children.top_down_role: Direction families whose primary role is restoration of path proximity.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The centering direction solves the primal-dual Newton system with complementarity right-hand side \(\sigma\mu\mathbf1-Xs\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible primal-dual Newton centering direction for standard-form linear programming.

source_refs.locator: Primal-Dual Methods: Development of the Fundamental Ideas p. 43

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a strictly positive primal-dual feasible point, choose \(0<\sigma\le1\), set \(\mu=x^{\mathsf T}s/n\), and compute \((\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta s)\) from \[A\Delta x=0,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}\Delta y+\Delta s=0,\qquad S\Delta x+X\Delta s=\sigma\mu\mathbf1-Xs.\] Choose a step length \(\alpha>0\) preserving \(x+\alpha\Delta x>0\) and \(s+\alpha\Delta s>0\), and output the updated point. The choice \(\sigma=1\) targets restoration toward the current-parameter central point; smaller \(\sigma\) also requests complementarity reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A centering direction is the primal-dual Newton step targeting uniform complementarity at a selected fraction of the current average.
knowledge_statements.title: Centering Directions

source_witnesses.locator: Primal-Dual Methods: Development of the Fundamental Ideas p. 43

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggregate-gap behavior of the pure feasible centering direction with target parameter unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\mu=x^{\mathsf T}s/n\) and the pure centering direction satisfies \[A\Delta x=0,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}\Delta y+\Delta s=0,\qquad S\Delta x+X\Delta s=\mu\mathbf1-Xs,\] then \(\Delta x^{\mathsf T}\Delta s=0\) and, for every common step length \(\alpha\), \[(x+\alpha\Delta x)^{\mathsf T}(s+\alpha\Delta s)=x^{\mathsf T}s.\] Thus pure centering can redistribute component products without changing their aggregate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pure feasible centering step redistributes complementary products while preserving their total.
assumptions_latex: The primal and slack updates use the same step length \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x+\alpha\Delta x)^{\mathsf T}(s+\alpha\Delta s)=x^{\mathsf T}s.
knowledge_statements.title: Pure Centering Preserves Aggregate Complementarity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The centering component of the practical LP predictor–corrector construction. The cubic rule is heuristic and has no stated analytical guarantee; the extract's separate second-order corrector is outside this partial placement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let K=\begin{bmatrix}0&A^T&I\\A&0&0\\S&0&X\end{bmatrix},\ X=\operatorname{Diag}(x),\ S=\operatorname{Diag}(s),\ \mu=x^Ts/n, and solve K\Delta^{\mathrm{aff}}=(-r_c,-r_b,-XSe)^T. Define \alpha_{\mathrm{aff}}^{\mathrm{pri}}=\min\!\left(1,\min_{i:\Delta x_i^{\mathrm{aff}}<0}-x_i/\Delta x_i^{\mathrm{aff}}\right) and \alpha_{\mathrm{aff}}^{\mathrm{dual}}=\min\!\left(1,\min_{i:\Delta s_i^{\mathrm{aff}}<0}-s_i/\Delta s_i^{\mathrm{aff}}\right). Then \mu_{\mathrm{aff}}=\frac{(x+\alpha_{\mathrm{aff}}^{\mathrm{pri}}\Delta x^{\mathrm{aff}})^T(s+\alpha_{\mathrm{aff}}^{\mathrm{dual}}\Delta s^{\mathrm{aff}})}{n},\qquad \sigma=\left(\frac{\mu_{\mathrm{aff}}}{\mu}\right)^3.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An uncentered affine predictor estimates the complementarity attainable at the largest nonnegative primal and dual affine steps. The ratio of this predicted complementarity to the current duality measure is cubed to choose the centering parameter. This is a practical heuristic, not an analytically justified guarantee.
assumptions_latex: \text{If a negative-component index set is empty, that variable imposes no finite positivity bound before the cap at }1.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sigma=\left(\mu_{\mathrm{aff}}/\mu\right)^3\quad\text{is the heuristic adaptive centering parameter.}
