knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Partition Identification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Threshold identification relative to a strictly complementary optimal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the primal-dual pair \\(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\\) and \\(\max\{b^Ty:A^Ty+s=c,\ s\geq0\}\\). Let \\(x^*,y^*,s^*\\) be strictly complementary and set \\(\delta=\min_i\max\{x_i^*,s_i^*\}>0\\). Given a feasible interior point \\(x,y,s\\) satisfying \\(\|x-x^*\|_\infty<\delta/2\\) and \\(\|s-s^*\|_\infty<\delta/2\\), output \\(B=\{i:x_i>\delta/2\}\\) and \\(N=\{i:s_i>\delta/2\}\\). Then \\(B=\{i:x_i^*>0\}\\), \\(N=\{i:s_i^*>0\}\\), and \\(B\dot\cup N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Thresholding a sufficiently accurate interior point recovers the positive primal and positive dual-slack index sets of a strictly complementary optimum.
assumptions_latex: \\(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\\) and the primal-dual pair has a strictly complementary optimum.
The supplied point is primal-dual feasible and strictly interior.
The stated uniform error bounds hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \\(B=\operatorname{supp}(x^*)\\), \\(N=\operatorname{supp}(s^*)\\), and \\(B\dot\cup N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\\).

notation.meaning: Primal-positive and dual-slack-positive parts of the optimal partition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Boundary Optimum Can Hide the Maximal Partition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of support-based identification from an arbitrary selected optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{0:x_1+x_2=1,\ x\ge0\}\), every feasible point is optimal and the maximal primal block is \(B=\{1,2\}\). The endpoint \(x^*=(1,0)\) has support \(\{1\}\). Thus convergence to or thresholding near this non-relative-interior optimum does not identify the maximal primal block.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{supp}(x^*)\ne B\text{ for }x^*=(1,0).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic and relative-interior formulations of the LP optimal partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X^*\) be the primal optimal set and \(\mathcal S^*\) the set of dual-optimal slack vectors. Define \(B=\{i:\exists x\in\mathcal X^*,\ x_i>0\}\) and \(N=\{i:\exists s\in\mathcal S^*,\ s_i>0\}\). Then \(B\cap N=\varnothing\). For \(x^{ri}\in\operatorname{ri}(\mathcal X^*)\) and \(s^{ri}\in\operatorname{ri}(\mathcal S^*)\), \(B=\{i:x_i^{ri}>0\}\) and \(N=\{i:s_i^{ri}>0\}\). A strictly complementary optimal pair satisfies \(B\mathbin{\dot\cup}N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximal optimal partition records coordinates positive somewhere on the primal and dual optimal faces; relative-interior optima reveal both blocks.
assumptions_latex: The primal and dual optimal sets are nonempty.
Relative interiors are taken in the respective affine hulls.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B=\operatorname{supp}(x^{ri}),\quad N=\operatorname{supp}(s^{ri}),\quad B\cap N=\varnothing.

children.title: Optimal-Basis Recovery
children.top_down_role: Recovery of a basic optimal solution from an interior approximation.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Basis Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite recovery by solving and verifying candidate bases selected from an identified partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \\(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\\), assume \\(A\\) has full row rank and the optimal partition \\(B\\) is known. Enumerate sets \\(I\subseteq B\\) with \\( |I|=m\\) and nonsingular \\(A_I\\). For each set solve \\(A_Ix_I=b\\), set \\(x_{I^c}=0\\), solve \\(A_I^Ty=c_I\\), and set \\(s=c-A^Ty\\). Output the first candidate satisfying \\(x_I\geq0\\) and \\(s\geq0\\). If an optimal basic feasible solution supported in \\(B\\) exists, the enumeration terminates with a primal-dual feasible complementary pair and hence an optimal basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumerating nonsingular column subsets of the identified primal partition and checking feasibility and reduced costs recovers an optimal basis.
assumptions_latex: The set \\(B\\) is the correctly identified primal part of an optimal partition.
An optimal basic feasible solution has support contained in \\(B\\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned \\(I\\) is an optimal basis, and the constructed \\(x,y,s\\) is primal-dual optimal.

notation.meaning: Submatrix formed by columns indexed by the candidate basis.
Primal part of the optimal partition.

source_refs.locator: 8.5 Analysis of Karmarkar's Algorithm: Convergence, Complexity, Sliding Objective Method, and Basic Optimal Solutions p. 417

source_witnesses.locator: 8.5 Analysis of Karmarkar's Algorithm: Convergence, Complexity, Sliding Objective Method, and Basic Optimal Solutions p. 417

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact basis recovery allowing zero-valued basic variables outside the primal-positive partition block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) with \(\operatorname{rank}A=m\), let \(B\) be the maximal primal-positive optimal-partition block. Enumerate all \(m\)-element sets \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) for which \(A_I\) is nonsingular, optionally prioritizing sets containing many indices of \(B\). Compute \(x_I=A_I^{-1}b\), \(x_{I^c}=0\), \(y=A_I^{-\mathsf T}c_I\), and \(s=c-A^{\mathsf T}y\). Accept when \(x_I\ge0\), \(s_{I^c}\ge0\), and \(\operatorname{supp}(x)\subseteq B\). If the LP has an optimum, finite enumeration returns an optimal basis; indices in \(I\setminus B\) may be zero-valued degenerate basic variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partition-guided basis search must allow zero-valued basic indices outside the positive block and accept only after exact primal and reduced-cost tests.
assumptions_latex: The standard-form LP has an optimal solution.
\(B\) is the correctly identified maximal primal-positive partition block.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite enumeration returns an optimal basis while permitting \(I\setminus B\ne\varnothing\) at degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy-Aware Optimal-Basis Enumeration

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degenerate Bases Need Not Lie in the Positive Partition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of restricting basis indices to the primal-positive block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=I_2\), \(b=(1,0)^{\mathsf T}\), and \(c=0\). The unique feasible and optimal vector is \(x^*=(1,0)^{\mathsf T}\), so the maximal primal-positive block is \(B=\{1\}\). The only two-column basis is \(I=\{1,2\}\). Thus no \(I\subseteq B\) is a basis although an optimal basis exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degenerate optimal basis may require zero-valued basic indices outside the positive partition block.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Restricting candidate bases to \(I\subseteq B\) can fail under degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Bases Need Not Lie in the Positive Partition

knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Solution Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise rational reconstruction of a primal-dual LP solution under a known denominator bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the rational primal-dual pair \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\) and \(\max\{b^Ty:A^Ty+s=c,\ s\geq0\}\). Let \(z^*=(x^*,y^*,s^*)\in\mathbb{Q}^d\) be a primal-dual optimal solution whose reduced coordinate denominators are at most \(Q\geq1\). Given \(\widehat z\in\mathbb{R}^d\) satisfying \(\|\widehat z-z^*\|_\infty<1/(2Q^2)\), reconstruct each coordinate as the unique reduced fraction \(p/q\) with \(1\leq q\leq Q\) and \(|\widehat z_i-p/q|<1/(2Q^2)\). Using continued fractions to find these fractions and then verifying exactly that \(Ax=b\), \(A^Ty+s=c\), \(x\geq0\), \(s\geq0\), and \(x^Ts=0\) returns \(z^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sufficiently accurate approximation uniquely determines every bounded-denominator coordinate of a primal-dual rational optimum, after which exact feasibility and complementarity checks certify the recovered solution.
assumptions_latex: \(z^*=(x^*,y^*,s^*)\) is primal-dual optimal and every reduced coordinate denominator is at most \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Coordinatewise rational reconstruction followed by exact primal-dual verification returns \(z^*\).

notation.meaning: Known upper bound on reduced coordinate denominators.
Exact vector encoding the primal variables, dual multipliers, and dual slacks.
Approximation to the encoded primal-dual solution.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computational complexity when the approximation and LP data are rational binary inputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\widehat z\), \(Q\), and the rational LP data are given in binary, continued-fraction reconstruction of every coordinate with denominator at most \(Q\), followed by exact primal-dual verification, uses time polynomial in the total input bit length and the number of coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For rational binary inputs, continued-fraction reconstruction and exact LP verification have polynomial bit complexity.
assumptions_latex: \(\widehat z\in\mathbb Q^d\) and \(Q\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\) are binary encoded.
The reconstruction and verification use exact integer or rational arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{recover}}=\operatorname{poly}(\operatorname{size}(A,b,c,\widehat z,Q),d).
knowledge_statements.title: Bit Complexity of Bounded-Denominator Reconstruction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information-theoretic boundary for coordinatewise exact rational recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(r\in\mathbb Q\), there exists \(r'\in\mathbb Q\setminus\{r\}\) such that \(|r-r'|<\varepsilon\). Hence no positive error radius uniquely identifies an unrestricted rational coordinate. Coordinatewise exact recovery therefore requires a denominator bound, an equivalent separation bound, or additional exact constraints that isolate the candidate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite numerical accuracy cannot identify an unrestricted rational number without separation information or additional exact constraints.
assumptions_latex: Candidate rational coordinates may have arbitrarily large denominators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No positive error tolerance uniquely identifies every unrestricted rational coordinate.
knowledge_statements.title: Necessity of Rational Separation Information

children.title: Rational Bit Complexity
children.top_down_role: Encoded-data and rational-arithmetic complexity for LP path following.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional transfer from polynomial path-following arithmetic complexity to Turing bit complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a rational path-following implementation performs \(\operatorname{poly}(m,n,L,\log(1/\varepsilon))\) arithmetic steps, uses only \(\operatorname{poly}(m,n,L,\log(1/\varepsilon))\)-bit operands, and preserves positivity, neighborhood membership, and its progress inequality under rounding, then it reaches its \(\varepsilon\)-accuracy predicate in \(\operatorname{poly}(m,n,L,\log(1/\varepsilon))\) bit operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial path-following arithmetic complexity transfers to polynomial bit complexity only with polynomial working precision and polynomial-cost arithmetic.
assumptions_latex: The rational LP has dimensions \(m,n\) and binary input length \(L\).
The implementation executes polynomially many arithmetic steps in \(m,n,L,\log(1/\varepsilon)\).
Polynomial-bit rounding preserves positivity, neighborhood membership, and progress.
Operations on rounded operands have polynomial bit cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The \(\varepsilon\)-accuracy predicate is reached in \(\operatorname{poly}(m,n,L,\log(1/\varepsilon))\) bit operations.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Precision Transfer Principle

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Turing-model cost definition for rational LP path-following computations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a rational LP encoded in \(L\) bits, bit complexity is the number of elementary Boolean operations used to manipulate the encoded input, intermediate rational quantities, and output. If a computation performs \(N\) rational arithmetic operations on numerators and denominators of at most \(B\) bits, its bit cost depends on both \(N\) and \(B\); a polynomial bound on \(N\) alone is not a polynomial bit-complexity bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rational bit complexity depends on both the number of arithmetic operations and the sizes of intermediate rational operands.
assumptions_latex: The LP data and requested tolerance have finite binary encodings.
Intermediate rational values are represented by encoded numerators and denominators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bit complexity charges for both arithmetic-step count and operand bit lengths.

notation.meaning: Maximum intermediate numerator or denominator bit length.

knowledge_statements.title: Rational Path-Following Bit-Cost Model

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between approximate termination and exact rational LP recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A positive approximate duality-gap or residual bound is not by itself an exact optimality certificate and need not identify an optimal basis or a unique optimizer. Exact recovery requires an additional rational separation, denominator, basis-identification, or reconstruction theorem with a polynomially encoded threshold below which a verifiable exact optimum can be recovered.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small positive error alone does not justify exact recovery; a rational separation or reconstruction guarantee is required.
assumptions_latex: A path-following computation has reached a positive approximate gap or residual tolerance \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact recovery is justified only after an explicit polynomially encoded recovery threshold or equivalent guarantee is supplied.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Recovery Boundary
Rational Bit Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Turing-model complexity including operand lengths and exact rational recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a rational LP with \\(m\\) constraints, \\(n\\) variables, and binary input length \\(L\\), a rational implementation of a polynomial path-following method computes a primal-dual point with gap at most \\(\varepsilon>0\\) using \\(\operatorname{poly}(m,n,L,\log(1/\varepsilon))\\) bit operations, provided intermediate numbers are rounded to polynomially many bits while preserving the path neighborhood. Choosing \\(\log(1/\varepsilon)=\operatorname{poly}(m,n,L)\\) sufficiently large for rational reconstruction yields an exact optimal solution in overall polynomial bit complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rational path following is polynomial in dimensions, input encoding length, and logarithmic target accuracy, including controlled rounding and exact recovery.
assumptions_latex: The LP data are rational and have total binary encoding length \\(L\\).
A polynomial-time initialization or homogeneous embedding is available.
Rounding preserves the prescribed central-path neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The bit-operation count is \\(\operatorname{poly}(m,n,L,\log(1/\varepsilon))\\), and exact recovery remains polynomial for suitably small \\(\varepsilon\\).

notation.meaning: Total binary encoding length of the rational LP data.

children.title: Real-Arithmetic Complexity
children.top_down_role: Arithmetic-operation complexity independent of finite encoding details.

knowledge_statements.title: Real-Arithmetic Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-cost real-arithmetic bound for dense short-step path following.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the unit-cost real-RAM model, a feasible short-step primal-dual path-following method for an LP with \\(m\leq n\\) and full-row-rank constraint matrix reduces complementarity from \\(\mu_0\\) to at most \\(\varepsilon\\) in \\(O(\sqrt n\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon))\\) iterations. If each Newton direction is computed by forming and factoring a dense \\(m\times m\\) normal-equations matrix, each iteration costs \\(O(m^2n+m^3)\\) arithmetic operations. Thus the total real-arithmetic cost is \\(O((m^2n+m^3)\sqrt n\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon))\\), excluding bit lengths and numerical precision.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dense short-step path following uses logarithmically many accuracy stages, with total real-operation cost equal to iteration count times Newton-system cost.
assumptions_latex: The initial point is feasible and lies in the required short-step neighborhood.
\\(A\\) has full row rank and \\(m\leq n\\).
Exact real arithmetic has unit cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The total arithmetic cost is \\(O((m^2n+m^3)\sqrt n\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon))\\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-cost model underlying real-arithmetic complexity statements for LP path following.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the unit-cost real-arithmetic model, each scalar addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero scalar, and exact comparison costs one operation independently of operand magnitude or finite representability. Matrix operations are charged through their scalar primitives unless another oracle is explicitly declared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Real-arithmetic complexity counts exact scalar algebra and comparisons at unit cost, independently of encoding length and precision.
assumptions_latex: The computation is analyzed on an exact real-register machine.
Each listed scalar primitive has unit cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The count is an arithmetic-operation bound and makes no finite-precision or Boolean-time claim.

children.top_down_role: Separation of iteration counts from the cost of direction computation.

children.title: Iteration-Count Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity accounting based on the number of path-following iterations.

knowledge_statements.title: Iteration-Count Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Short-step iteration count measured by complementarity reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\geq1\) be the number of LP variables. Suppose a feasible primal-dual path-following sequence remains in a fixed short-step neighborhood and satisfies \(\mu_{k+1}\leq(1-\alpha/\sqrt n)\mu_k\) for every integer \(k\geq0\), where \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) is independent of \(n\) and \(k\). If \(\mu_0>\varepsilon>0\), then \(\mu_k\leq\varepsilon\) whenever \[k\geq\frac{\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon)}{-\log(1-\alpha/\sqrt n)}.\] Consequently, \(O(\sqrt n\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon))\) iterations suffice. This count treats a Newton direction and its neighborhood-preserving update as one iteration and excludes their arithmetic cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an LP with n variables, a uniform complementarity contraction of order one over the square root of n yields the standard short-step iteration bound, excluding per-iteration arithmetic work.
assumptions_latex: Every iterate remains in the prescribed neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At most \(O(\sqrt n\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon))\) iterations are required.

children.title: Direction-Computation Cost
children.top_down_role: Per-iteration arithmetic cost associated with computing search directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Direction-Computation Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense arithmetic cost of one primal-dual Newton direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a primal-dual LP iterate with positive diagonal matrices \\(X=\operatorname{Diag}(x)\\) and \\(S=\operatorname{Diag}(s)\\), eliminate the primal and slack directions to obtain a normal-equations system with coefficient matrix \\(M=AXS^{-1}A^T\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\\). When \\(m\leq n\\), dense formation of \\(M\\) costs \\(O(m^2n)\\) arithmetic operations, its Cholesky factorization costs \\(O(m^3)\\), and substitutions plus recovery of the remaining direction components cost no more than these leading terms. Hence one direction costs \\(O(m^2n+m^3)\\) real-arithmetic operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forming and factoring the dense normal equations dominates one primal-dual Newton direction, costing cubic constraint work plus matrix formation.
assumptions_latex: \\(A\\) has full row rank and \\(m\leq n\\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One Newton direction costs \\(O(m^2n+m^3)\\) arithmetic operations.

notation.meaning: Diagonal matrices of primal variables and dual slacks.

children.title: Aggregate Arithmetic Cost
children.top_down_role: Total arithmetic cost combining iteration counts with per-iteration work.

knowledge_statements.title: Aggregate Arithmetic Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product bound combining iteration count and per-direction arithmetic cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a path-following method require at most \\(K(n,\mu_0,\varepsilon)\\) iterations, and let direction computation, line search, and iterate update cost at most \\(C(m,n)\\) arithmetic operations per iteration. Its aggregate real-arithmetic cost is \\(O(KC)\\). In particular, combining \\(K=O(\sqrt n\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon))\\) with dense normal-equations cost \\(C=O(m^2n+m^3)\\) gives \\[O\!\left((m^2n+m^3)\sqrt n\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon)\right).\\] Initialization and exact-solution recovery must be added separately when they are not covered by the per-iteration bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total real-arithmetic work is the iteration bound times per-iteration work, plus any separately charged initialization and recovery costs.
assumptions_latex: The iteration and direction-cost bounds hold uniformly over all generated iterates.
Non-direction work per iteration is absorbed by \\(C(m,n)\\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The dense aggregate cost is \\(O((m^2n+m^3)\sqrt n\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon))\\), apart from separately charged phases.

children.title: Strong-Polynomiality Boundary
children.top_down_role: The boundary between polynomial-time LP interior-point methods and strongly polynomial algorithms.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Polynomiality Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why ordinary path-following polynomiality does not by itself establish strong polynomiality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For rational linear programming with \(m\) constraints, \(n\) variables, and binary input length \(L\), a strongly polynomial algorithm must use a number of arithmetic operations bounded by a polynomial in \(m+n\), independently of the numerical data and \(L\), and its intermediate rational numbers must have encoding lengths polynomial in \(L\). Therefore, a path-following analysis whose operation bound contains \(L\), \(\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon)\), a condition measure, or a denominator bound that has not itself been bounded by \(\operatorname{poly}(m+n)\) independently of the data does not establish strong polynomiality. In particular, choosing \(\varepsilon=2^{-\operatorname{poly}(L)}\) to obtain exact recovery can establish ordinary polynomial bit complexity but does not make that analysis strongly polynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A path-following analysis proves strong polynomiality only if all operation-count factors are bounded polynomially in the dimensions independently of data values and encoding length; accuracy chosen from the input length generally proves only ordinary polynomial bit complexity.
assumptions_latex: The problem is rational linear programming with dimensions \(m,n\) and input length \(L\).
At least one factor in the analyzed operation bound lacks a polynomial bound in \(m+n\) that is independent of the numerical data and \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated path-following bound establishes at most ordinary polynomiality and does not, by itself, establish strong polynomiality.

children.title: Neighborhood-Invariant Analysis
children.top_down_role: Complexity analyses based on controlled path proximity.

knowledge_statements.title: Neighborhood-Invariant Analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomiality from invariance of a fixed central-path neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an LP with \(n\geq1\) variables, let \((x,y,s)\) be primal-dual feasible with \(x>0\) and \(s>0\), define \(X=\operatorname{Diag}(x)\), \(S=\operatorname{Diag}(s)\), \(e=(1,\ldots,1)^T\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(\mu=x^Ts/n\). For fixed \(\theta\in(0,1)\), let \(N_2(\theta)\) be the set of such feasible interior points satisfying \(\|XSe-\mu e\|_2\leq\theta\mu\). Suppose a constant \(\alpha>0\), independent of the instance and iteration, is such that every prescribed Newton update from \(N_2(\theta)\) remains in \(N_2(\theta)\) and satisfies \(\mu^+\leq(1-\alpha/\sqrt n)\mu\). Starting in \(N_2(\theta)\), all iterates remain in that neighborhood and the method reaches \(\mu\leq\varepsilon\) in \(O(\sqrt n\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon))\) iterations for \(0<\varepsilon<\mu_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an LP with n variables, invariance of a fixed feasible central-path neighborhood together with uniform complementarity reduction yields the standard polynomial iteration bound.
assumptions_latex: The initial primal-dual feasible interior point belongs to \(N_2(\theta)\).
Each update gives the stated complementarity contraction with an instance-independent \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every iterate remains in \(N_2(\theta)\), and \(O(\sqrt n\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon))\) iterations suffice.

notation.meaning: Euclidean neighborhood of primal-dual feasible interior points.
Diagonal matrices formed from the primal variables and dual slacks.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary of a neighborhood-invariant complexity proof; departure does not itself imply divergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the applicable progress theorem is established only for iterates in a set \(N\). If an accepted update produces \(z^+\notin N\), the theorem supplies no guarantee for the subsequent update unless membership in an applicable invariant domain is restored. This invalidates continuation of that neighborhood-based proof, but does not by itself imply divergence of the algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Leaving the controlled neighborhood breaks the induction behind its complexity proof, without necessarily causing algorithmic divergence.
assumptions_latex: A local progress theorem is known only for iterates in a set \(N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The local theorem cannot justify subsequent progress from \(z^+\) until an applicable invariant is restored.

notation.meaning: Neighborhood on which the local path-following estimates apply.

children.title: Uniform Progress Analysis
children.top_down_role: Complexity analyses based on per-iteration barrier or gap progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Progress Analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration bounds obtained from uniform multiplicative reduction of complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\geq1\) be the number of LP variables, and let \(\mu_k>0\) be the barrier parameter or average complementarity at iteration \(k\geq0\). If there is a constant \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), independent of \(n\) and \(k\), such that \(\mu_{k+1}\leq(1-\alpha/\sqrt n)\mu_k\) at every iteration before termination, then \(\mu_k\leq(1-\alpha/\sqrt n)^k\mu_0\). For \(0<\varepsilon<\mu_0\), an iterate satisfying \(\mu_k\leq\varepsilon\) is therefore obtained within \(\left\lceil\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon)/[-\log(1-\alpha/\sqrt n)]\right\rceil\) iterations, which is \(O(\sqrt n\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an LP with n variables, uniform multiplicative progress in complementarity yields a logarithmic-accuracy iteration bound of order square root of n.
assumptions_latex: The contraction factor \(1-\alpha/\sqrt n\) holds uniformly before termination for a fixed \(\alpha\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stopping time is \(O(\sqrt n\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon))\).

notation.meaning: Barrier parameter or average complementarity at iteration k.

source_refs.locator: A General Complexity Theorem for Path-Following Methods p. 61

source_witnesses.locator: A General Complexity Theorem for Path-Following Methods p. 61

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variable-rate form of multiplicative progress; a dimension-dependent bound requires corresponding accumulated progress.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(E_0>0\) and \(E_{k+1}\le(1-\delta_k)E_k\) with \(0<\delta_k<1\), then
\[
E_K\le E_0\exp\!\left(-\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\delta_k\right).
\]
Therefore \(\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\delta_k\ge\log(E_0/\varepsilon)\) suffices for \(E_K\le\varepsilon\). In particular, \(\delta_k\ge c/\sqrt n\) yields the usual square-root-dimension logarithmic count, whereas positivity of the \(\delta_k\) alone does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonuniform multiplicative reductions, complexity is governed by accumulated relative progress.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_K\le E_0\exp(-\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\delta_k)\), so accumulated progress \(\log(E_0/\varepsilon)\) suffices for tolerance \(\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Relative progress achieved at iteration k.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Rate Multiplicative Progress Criterion

children.title: Initial Proximity-Accuracy Scaling
children.top_down_role: The role of initial proximity and requested solution accuracy in iteration bounds.

children.title: Initial-Proximity Dependence
children.top_down_role: Iteration-bound sensitivity to the quality of the initial point.

knowledge_statements.title: Initial-Proximity Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of path-following iterations on the initial complementarity scale after neighborhood initialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\geq1\) be the number of LP variables. Assume an initial feasible interior point belongs to the invariant path neighborhood and has complementarity \(\mu_0>0\), and suppose every iteration satisfies \(\mu_{k+1}\leq(1-\alpha/\sqrt n)\mu_k\) for a fixed \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). For any target \(0<\varepsilon<\mu_0\), the stopping time \(K\) satisfies \[K\leq\left\lceil\frac{\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon)}{-\log(1-\alpha/\sqrt n)}\right\rceil=O\!\left(\sqrt n\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon)\right).\] Thus, for fixed \(\varepsilon\), dependence on the initial complementarity scale is logarithmic after neighborhood membership has been established. The work required to obtain such an initial point is a separate initialization cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After a feasible point has entered the invariant neighborhood, the iteration bound depends logarithmically on the ratio of its initial complementarity to the target complementarity; initialization is charged separately.
assumptions_latex: The initial point belongs to the required invariant neighborhood.
The stated uniform contraction holds with fixed \(\alpha\in(0,1)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(E_{k+1}\le (1-c/\sqrt{\nu})E_k\), then \(E_k\le E_0\exp(-ck/\sqrt{\nu})\). Consequently, the condition \(E_K\le\varepsilon\) is guaranteed whenever
\[
K\ge \frac{\sqrt{\nu}}{c}\log\!\left(\frac{E_0}{\varepsilon}\right).
\]
Thus the dependence on target accuracy is logarithmic: with \(E_0\) and \(\nu\) fixed, reducing the tolerance from a constant to \(\varepsilon\) requires \(O(\log(1/\varepsilon))\) iterations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accuracy floor for an inexact path-following contraction, without asserting a particular finite-precision model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(E_0\ge0\) and \(E_{k+1}\le(1-\delta)E_k+\eta\) with \(0<\delta<1\) and \(\eta\ge0\), then
\[
E_k\le(1-\delta)^kE_0+\frac{\eta}{\delta}.
\]
Thus this recursion alone does not guarantee attainment of arbitrary tolerances at or below the persistent-error scale \(\eta/\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A persistent additive error creates an accuracy floor, so multiplicative progress no longer guarantees arbitrarily small target accuracy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_k\le(1-\delta)^kE_0+\eta/\delta\), and the estimate alone cannot guarantee arbitrary accuracy below the scale \(\eta/\delta\).

knowledge_statements.title: Short-Step Neighborhood-Invariance Analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible primal-dual short-step method using the Euclidean central-path neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta s)\) solve
\[
A\Delta x=0,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}\Delta y+\Delta s=0,\qquad S\Delta x+X\Delta s=\sigma\mu e-XSe.
\]
There exist universal constants \(\theta_0,\delta_0>0\) such that, whenever \(0<\theta\le\theta_0\) and \(0<\delta\le\delta_0\), the full iterate \((x^+,y^+,s^+)=(x,y,s)+(\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta s)\) satisfies \(x^+,s^+>0\) and \((x^+,y^+,s^+)\in\mathcal N_2(\theta)\). Thus the short-step update preserves the prescribed centrality neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a sufficiently small centering reduction, a full primal-dual Newton step preserves positivity and the narrow Euclidean centrality neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has full row rank, \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and \((x,y,s)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^n\) is strictly feasible with \(Ax=b\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), and \(x,s>0\).
\((x,y,s)\in\mathcal N_2(\theta)\) for a sufficiently small universal \(\theta>0\).
The centering parameter is \(\sigma=1-\delta/\sqrt n\) for a sufficiently small universal \(\delta>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The full Newton iterate is positive and remains in \(\mathcal N_2(\theta)\).

notation.meaning: Diagonal matrices formed from x and s.

For the full trial iterate, \[\Delta x^{\mathsf T}\Delta s=0,\qquad \mu^+=\sigma\mu,\qquad X^+S^+e-\mu^+e=\Delta X\Delta S e.\] Thus its centrality error is exactly the quadratic complementarity remainder.

knowledge_statements.title: Short-Step Complementarity-Progress Analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-iteration complementarity decrease for feasible short-step primal-dual path following.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For universal constants chosen so that the short-step neighborhood is invariant, the updated average complementarity obeys
\[
\mu_{k+1}\le\left(1-\frac{c}{\sqrt n}\right)\mu_k
\]
for some universal \(c>0\). Iteration therefore gives
\[
\mu_k\le\mu_0\exp\!\left(-\frac{ck}{\sqrt n}\right).
\]
Because primal and dual feasibility are preserved, \(x_k^{\mathsf T}s_k=n\mu_k\) is the primal-dual objective gap; hence this contraction is also a certified objective-gap reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each invariant short step reduces average complementarity by a factor of the form 1−c/√n while preserving primal and dual feasibility.
assumptions_latex: The hypotheses of short-step neighborhood invariance hold at iteration \(k\).
A full primal-dual Newton step uses \(\sigma=1-\delta/\sqrt n\), where \(\delta>0\) is a sufficiently small universal constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu_{k+1}\le(1-c/\sqrt n)\mu_k\) for a universal \(c>0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasibility Boundary of the Gap Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of interpreting short-step complementarity progress as certified objective-gap progress.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the standard-form primal-dual pair, define \(r_p=Ax-b\) and \(r_d=A^Ty+s-c\). Then
\[
c^Tx-b^Ty=x^Ts-x^Tr_d+y^Tr_p.
\]
Consequently \(x^Ts=n\mu\) equals the primal-dual objective gap under exact primal and dual feasibility. For infeasible iterates, complementarity contraction alone does not certify objective-gap contraction unless the residual terms are also controlled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementarity contraction certifies objective-gap contraction only for primal-dual feasible iterates; infeasible iterates also require residual control.
assumptions_latex: The primal problem is \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) and the dual is \(\max\{b^Ty:A^Ty+s=c,\ s\ge0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c^Tx-b^Ty=x^Ts-x^Tr_d+y^Tr_p\); hence \(x^Ts=n\mu\) is the objective gap when \(r_p=r_d=0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Boundary of the Gap Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any fixed reduction factor \(q\in(0,1)\), the contraction yields \(\mu_k\le q\mu_0\) once
\[
k\ge \frac{\sqrt n}{c}\log\!\left(\frac1q\right).
\]
Since \(q\) is fixed, the required number of Newton iterations is \(O(\sqrt n)\). Thus the short-step dimension dependence is the square root of the number of complementary pairs, equivalently the square root of the logarithmic barrier parameter for the standard nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-factor complementarity reduction takes O(√n) short-step Newton iterations.

For an accepted \(\alpha\in[0,1]\), set \((x^+,y^+,s^+)=(x,y,s)+\alpha(\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta s)\). Then \(\Delta x^{\mathsf T}\Delta s=0\) and \[\mu^+=\bigl(1-\alpha(1-\sigma)\bigr)\mu.\] Consequently, if wide-neighborhood preservation guarantees \(\alpha\ge a_\gamma/n\) and \(\sigma\le\bar\sigma<1\), then \(\mu^+\le(1-c_\gamma/n)\mu\), where \(c_\gamma=a_\gamma(1-\bar\sigma)>0\).

children.title: Long-Step Centrality-Recovery Analysis
children.top_down_role: Complexity analyses for restoring centrality after aggressive movement.

assumptions_latex: After a target-parameter reduction, the strictly feasible iterate has centrality measure \(D_0<\infty\).
A centering Newton iteration satisfies \(D_{j+1}\le\rho D_j\) whenever \(D_j>\theta\), for fixed \(0<\rho<1\) and target radius \(\theta>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At most \(\lceil\log(D_0/\theta)/\log(1/\rho)\rceil_+\) centering iterations restore \(D_j\le\theta\).

notation.meaning: Nonnegative centrality deviation after j recovery steps.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract contraction form of centrality recovery after an aggressive barrier-parameter update.

source_refs.locator: A Long-Step Path-Following Algorithm p. 96

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Repeated application of the recovery contraction gives \(D_j\le\rho^jD_0\). Hence the first index satisfying \(D_j\le\theta\) is bounded by
\[
j\le\left\lceil\frac{\log(D_0/\theta)}{\log(1/\rho)}\right\rceil_+,
\]
where \(\lceil t\rceil_+=\max\{0,\lceil t\rceil\}\). Thus an aggressive movement that increases centrality deviation to \(D_0\) can be followed by a logarithmically bounded recovery phase, provided every centering step has a uniform contraction factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniformly contracting centering iterations restore the required neighborhood in logarithmically many recovery steps.
knowledge_statements.title: Long-Step Centrality-Recovery Analysis

source_witnesses.locator: A Long-Step Path-Following Algorithm p. 96

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniformity boundary for converting phasewise recovery convergence into a polynomial worst-case bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For phase-dependent recovery satisfying \(D_{j+1,\ell}\le\rho_\ell D_{j,\ell}\), with \(0<\rho_\ell<1\), the phase-\(\ell\) recovery count is bounded by
\[
R_\ell=\left\lceil\frac{\log_+(D_{0,\ell}/\theta)}{\log(1/\rho_\ell)}\right\rceil,
\qquad \log_+(t)=\max\{0,\log t\}.
\]
Finite \(D_{0,\ell}\) and pointwise \(\rho_\ell<1\) ensure finite recovery in each fixed phase, but a uniform polynomial bound additionally requires uniform polynomial control of this ratio.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite recovery phase by phase does not imply uniformly polynomial recovery; initial deviations and contraction factors must be uniformly controlled.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A uniform polynomial recovery bound requires uniform polynomial control of \(\log_+(D_{0,\ell}/\theta)/\log(1/\rho_\ell)\).

notation.meaning: Initial centrality deviation in phase l.

assumptions_latex: Each outer update reduces the barrier target by a fixed factor \(q\in(0,1)\).
After every outer update, at most \(R(n)\) Newton centering iterations restore the prescribed neighborhood.
The initial and final targets satisfy \(0<\varepsilon<\mu_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method uses at most \(R(n)\lceil\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon)/\log(1/q)\rceil\) inner Newton iterations.

notation.meaning: Barrier or complementarity target after outer update ℓ.
Worst-case recentering iterations per outer update.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic accounting principle separating large target updates from their recentering work.

source_refs.locator: A General Complexity Theorem for Path-Following Methods p. 61
A Long-Step Path-Following Algorithm p. 96

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The number of outer updates required for \(\mu^{(L)}\le\varepsilon\) is
\[
L=\left\lceil\frac{\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon)}{\log(1/q)}\right\rceil.
\]
If every update requires at most \(R(n)\) recentering steps, the total number of inner Newton iterations is at most \(L R(n)\). Thus the accuracy dependence is carried by the outer logarithm, while the dimension and neighborhood-recovery costs are isolated in \(R(n)\); adding one target-update operation per phase gives total work proportional to \(L(1+R(n))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Large-update complexity equals the number of geometric target reductions times the worst-case recentering cost per reduction.
knowledge_statements.title: Large-Update Inner–Outer Complexity

source_witnesses.locator: A General Complexity Theorem for Path-Following Methods p. 61
A Long-Step Path-Following Algorithm p. 96

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonuniform extension of inner-outer accounting without asserting method-specific phase or recovery bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If phase \(\ell\) changes the target by \(\mu^{(\ell+1)}=q_\ell\mu^{(\ell)}\), where \(0<q_\ell<1\), and uses at most \(R_\ell\) recovery iterations, then after \(L\) phases
\[
\mu^{(L)}=\mu_0\prod_{\ell=0}^{L-1}q_\ell,
\qquad
\log\frac{\mu_0}{\mu^{(L)}}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{L-1}\log\frac1{q_\ell},
\]
and total inner work is at most \(\sum_{\ell=0}^{L-1}R_\ell\). The fixed-factor product bound is the uniform special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With variable large updates, logarithmic target reductions and phase recovery costs accumulate separately.
assumptions_latex: Phase \(\ell\) uses at most \(R_\ell\ge0\) inner recovery iterations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu^{(L)}=\mu_0\prod_{\ell=0}^{L-1}q_\ell\), and total inner iterations are at most \(\sum_{\ell=0}^{L-1}R_\ell\).

notation.meaning: Barrier or complementarity target at outer phase l.
Recovery iterations charged to phase l.

knowledge_statements.title: Narrow-Neighborhood Iteration Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration family induced by fixed-radius Euclidean centrality control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Neighborhood invariance permits every accepted update to be a full Newton step, and complementarity contraction gives
\[
x_k^{\mathsf T}s_k\le x_0^{\mathsf T}s_0\exp\!\left(-\frac{ck}{\sqrt n}\right).
\]
It follows that
\[
K\ge\frac{\sqrt n}{c}\log\!\left(\frac{x_0^{\mathsf T}s_0}{\varepsilon}\right)
\]
suffices for termination. Hence fixed narrow-neighborhood control produces the classical \(O(\sqrt n\log((x_0^{\mathsf T}s_0)/\varepsilon))\) iteration family in the Newton-step oracle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed narrow-neighborhood control yields the classical O(√n log(g₀/ε)) Newton-iteration bound.
assumptions_latex: The primal-dual iterates are strictly feasible and remain in a fixed Euclidean narrow neighborhood \(\mathcal N_2(\theta)\).
A full Newton step contracts average complementarity by \(1-c/\sqrt n\), with fixed \(c>0\).
The stopping rule is \(x_k^{\mathsf T}s_k\le\varepsilon\), where \(0<\varepsilon<x_0^{\mathsf T}s_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K=O\!\left(\sqrt n\log((x_0^{\mathsf T}s_0)/\varepsilon)\right)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Wide-Neighborhood Iteration Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration family induced by fixed componentwise wide-neighborhood control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The componentwise neighborhood and assumed long-step progress imply
\[
x_k^{\mathsf T}s_k\le x_0^{\mathsf T}s_0\exp\!\left(-\frac{c_\gamma k}{n}\right).
\]
Therefore
\[
K\ge\frac{n}{c_\gamma}\log\!\left(\frac{x_0^{\mathsf T}s_0}{\varepsilon}\right)
\]
suffices to reach the prescribed objective-gap tolerance. In the Newton-step oracle model, fixed wide-neighborhood control consequently yields an \(O(n\log((x_0^{\mathsf T}s_0)/\varepsilon))\) worst-case iteration family, with constants depending on \(\gamma\) but not on the requested accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed componentwise wide-neighborhood control yields an O(n log(g₀/ε)) worst-case Newton-iteration bound.
assumptions_latex: The primal-dual iterates are strictly feasible and remain in \(\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)\) for fixed \(\gamma\in(0,1)\).
Each accepted long step contracts complementarity by \(1-c_\gamma/n\), where \(c_\gamma>0\) is independent of \(n\) and \(k\).
The stopping rule is \(x_k^{\mathsf T}s_k\le\varepsilon\), where \(0<\varepsilon<x_0^{\mathsf T}s_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K=O\!\left(n\log((x_0^{\mathsf T}s_0)/\varepsilon)\right)\).

children.title: Adaptive-Update Iteration Bounds
children.top_down_role: Iteration bounds for methods varying update size through path progress.

assumptions_latex: Every accepted adaptive update preserves its prescribed centrality invariant and satisfies \(\mu_{k+1}\le\sigma_k\mu_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any \(N\) with \(\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}-\log\sigma_k\ge\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon)\) guarantees \(\mu_N\le\varepsilon\); if \(\sigma_k\le1-\delta/\sqrt n\) uniformly, the first stopping index is at most \(\left\lceil\delta^{-1}\sqrt n\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon)\right\rceil\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract iteration bound for accepted adaptive updates with quantified progress; it does not assert that a particular adaptive rule satisfies the invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every integer \(N\ge1\), \[\mu_N\le\mu_0\prod_{k=0}^{N-1}\sigma_k.\] Consequently, \(\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}-\log\sigma_k\ge\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon)\) is sufficient for \(\mu_N\le\varepsilon\). In particular, if \(\sigma_k\le1-\delta/\sqrt n\) for a constant \(0<\delta<1\), then the least index \(K\) satisfying \(\mu_K\le\varepsilon\) obeys \[K\le\left\lceil\frac{\sqrt n}{\delta}\log\!\left(\frac{\mu_0}{\varepsilon}\right)\right\rceil.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptive updates have the standard logarithmic bound when their accepted contraction factors provide sufficient cumulative progress; a uniform order-one-over-square-root-n reduction gives the classical square-root bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Cumulative-Progress Bound for Adaptive Updates

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict decrease at every adaptive iteration does not imply convergence to zero or a finite tolerance bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary when adaptive reductions become summably small.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\sigma_k=1-2^{-k-2}\) and \(\mu_{k+1}=\sigma_k\mu_k\). Then every iteration strictly decreases \(\mu_k\), but the infinite product \(L=\prod_{k=0}^{\infty}\sigma_k\) is positive, so \(\mu_k\downarrow L\mu_0>0\). Hence no iteration reaches any tolerance \(0<\varepsilon<L\mu_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptive steps can decrease complementarity at every iteration yet fail to approach zero when their reductions become summably small.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure Without Cumulative Adaptive Progress

assumptions_latex: Each adaptive step preserves the prescribed centrality neighborhood and satisfies \(\mu_{k+1}\le \sigma_k\mu_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\le \left\lceil \delta^{-1}\sqrt n\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon)\right\rceil\) whenever \(\sigma_k\le 1-\delta/\sqrt n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional bound for adaptive reductions that uniformly preserve a centrality neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be the least integer for which \(\mu_K\le\varepsilon\). Iterationwise contraction gives \(\mu_K\le\mu_0\prod_{k=0}^{K-1}\sigma_k\), so any \(K\) satisfying \(\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}-\log\sigma_k\ge\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon)\) suffices. In particular, if every adaptive choice obeys \(\sigma_k\le 1-\delta/\sqrt n\) for a constant \(0<\delta<1\), then \(K\le\left\lceil \delta^{-1}\sqrt n\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon)\right\rceil\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptive updates retain the standard path-following bound when every accepted update gives a uniform order-one-over-square-root-n reduction while preserving centrality.
knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive-Update Iteration Bounds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional contraction calculation is mathematically standard, but no source supports the adaptive neighborhood invariant. The statement also uses K first as the least stopping index and then as an arbitrary sufficient index, and includes a derivation rather than only the bound.

children.title: Switching-Neighborhood Iteration Bounds
children.top_down_role: Iteration bounds for methods assigning distinct roles to multiple neighborhoods.

assumptions_latex: There are \(q\ge1\) consecutive regimes with thresholds \(\mu_0>\mu_1>\cdots>\mu_q=\varepsilon>0\).
At the start of regime \(j\), the current measure is at most \(\mu_{j-1}\) and the iterate belongs to that regime's neighborhood.
Every progress iteration in regime \(j\) preserves that neighborhood and satisfies \(\mu^+\le(1-\delta_j/\sqrt n)\mu\), where \(0<\delta_j<1\).
Iterations used solely to enter a new regime's neighborhood are excluded from \(K_{\mathrm{prog}}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_{\mathrm{prog}}\le\sum_{j=1}^{q}\left\lceil\delta_j^{-1}\sqrt n\log(\mu_{j-1}/\mu_j)\right\rceil\).

notation.meaning: Target complementarity threshold ending regime j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive progress bound for a specified finite schedule of invariant centrality regimes; transition restoration is counted separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated threshold and invariance convention, the number of progress iterations used while regime \(j\) reduces the measure from at most \(\mu_{j-1}\) to at most \(\mu_j\) is at most \[\left\lceil\frac{\sqrt n}{\delta_j}\log\!\left(\frac{\mu_{j-1}}{\mu_j}\right)\right\rceil.\] Therefore \[K_{\mathrm{prog}}\le\sum_{j=1}^{q}\left\lceil\frac{\sqrt n}{\delta_j}\log\!\left(\frac{\mu_{j-1}}{\mu_j}\right)\right\rceil.\] In particular, if \(q\) is constant and \(\delta_j\ge\underline\delta>0\), then \(K_{\mathrm{prog}}=O(\sqrt n\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite sequence of invariant neighborhood regimes, the progress-iteration count is the sum of the regime-specific contraction bounds; restoration iterations are separate.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Additive Progress Bound for Switching Neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.title: Additive Progress Bound for Switching Neighborhoods

assumptions_latex: There are \(q\ge1\) consecutive neighborhood regimes, with initial measure \(\mu_0\) and target \(0<\varepsilon<\mu_0\).
Within regime \(j\), each accepted iteration preserves that regime and contracts \(\mu\) by at most \(1-\delta_j/\sqrt n\), where \(0<\delta_j<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_{\mathrm{prog}}\le\sum_{j=1}^{q}\left\lceil \delta_j^{-1}\sqrt n\log(\mu_{j-1}/\mu_j)\right\rceil\).

notation.meaning: duality measure at the end of regime j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive progress bound for a finite schedule of centrality neighborhoods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose thresholds \(\mu_0>\mu_1>\cdots>\mu_q=\varepsilon\). If regime \(j\) is used while reducing the measure from \(\mu_{j-1}\) to \(\mu_j\), its progress iterations are at most \(\left\lceil \delta_j^{-1}\sqrt n\log(\mu_{j-1}/\mu_j)\right\rceil\). Consequently the total number of progress iterations is bounded by the sum over regimes. Iterations used solely to restore membership after a switch are excluded and constitute transition overhead.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finitely many neighborhood regimes, the progress bound is the sum of each regime's contraction bound; restoration work at switches is counted separately.
knowledge_statements.title: Switching-Neighborhood Iteration Bounds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The additive calculation is plausible under the declared per-regime contractions, but no cited theorem supports the switching-neighborhood model, threshold convention, or exclusion of restoration iterations. The statement also contains derivational text.

children.title: Regime-Transition Overhead
children.top_down_role: Complexity contributions associated with transitions between neighborhood regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Regime-Transition Overhead
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accounting bound separating neighborhood-switch restoration from ordinary progress iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a run with \(q\ge 1\) consecutive regimes, let \(K_{\mathrm{prog}}\) be its number of progress iterations and suppose that the restoration following switch \(j\) uses at most \(r_j\) iterations. Then \(K_{\mathrm{total}}\le K_{\mathrm{prog}}+\sum_{j=1}^{q-1}r_j\). If \(r_j\le R\) for every switch, then \(K_{\mathrm{total}}\le K_{\mathrm{prog}}+R(q-1)\). If both \(R\) and \(q\) are independent of \(n\), \(\mu_0\), and \(\varepsilon\), this overhead does not change an \(O(\sqrt n\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon))\) progress order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transition overhead is at most the sum of the per-switch restoration bounds. Uniformly constant restoration cost across a constant number of regimes preserves the usual asymptotic progress order.
assumptions_latex: A run uses \(q\ge1\) consecutive regimes and makes \(q-1\) switches.
After switch \(j\), at most \(r_j\ge0\) iterations are used solely to enter the next regime's neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_{\mathrm{total}}\le K_{\mathrm{prog}}+\sum_{j=1}^{q-1}r_j\), and \(K_{\mathrm{total}}\le K_{\mathrm{prog}}+R(q-1)\) if \(r_j\le R\).

notation.meaning: iterations producing the within-regime progress bound
upper bound on restoration iterations following switch j

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Predictor-Corrector Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical polynomial bound under explicit predictor reduction and corrector neighborhood-restoration invariants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) count complete predictor-corrector cycles, with each predictor and its neighborhood-restoring corrector treated as one cycle. If \(\mu_{k+1}\le(1-\delta/\sqrt n)\mu_k\) for every cycle, where \(0<\delta<1\), then \(K\le\left\lceil\delta^{-1}\sqrt n\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon)\right\rceil\) cycles suffice to obtain \(\mu_K\le\varepsilon\). If each cycle uses a uniformly bounded number of Newton systems, the Newton-iteration order is also \(O(\sqrt n\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A predictor-corrector method has the standard square-root-dimension logarithmic bound when every complete cycle restores centrality and produces the stated uniform complementarity reduction.
assumptions_latex: The primal-dual LP has a strictly feasible starting point in a fixed centrality neighborhood.
Each predictor-corrector cycle restores that neighborhood and yields \(\mu_{k+1}\le(1-\delta/\sqrt n)\mu_k\) for some constant \(0<\delta<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\le\left\lceil\delta^{-1}\sqrt n\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon)\right\rceil\) predictor-corrector cycles suffice for \(\mu_K\le\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose a short-step method for a homogeneous self-dual embedding preserves a fixed central neighborhood and satisfies \(\eta_{k+1}\le(1-\delta/\sqrt
u)\eta_k\) at every iteration, where \(0<\delta<1\). Then \(K\le\left\lceil\delta^{-1}\sqrt
u\log(\eta_0/\varepsilon)ightceil\) iterations suffice to obtain \(\eta_K\le\varepsilon\). When the embedding barrier parameter satisfies \(
u=O(n)\), the bound is \(O(\sqrt n\log(\eta_0/\varepsilon))\).

A short-step method starts in a fixed central neighborhood and reduces its embedding parameter by a factor at most \(1-\delta/\sqrt\nu\) per iteration.

assumptions_latex: An order-\(p\) path model preserves its prescribed neighborhood after every accepted step.
For constants \(c>0\) and \(\alpha_p\ge0\), accepted steps satisfy \(\mu_{k+1}\le(1-c n^{-\alpha_p})\mu_k\), with \(0<c n^{-\alpha_p}<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\le\left\lceil c^{-1}n^{\alpha_p}\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon)\right\rceil\) suffices for \(\mu_K\le\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: order of the local path model
dimension exponent delivered by the model analysis

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-independent contraction template; the exponent must come from a specific higher-order method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated contraction, \(\mu_K\le(1-c n^{-\alpha_p})^K\mu_0\le\exp(-cKn^{-\alpha_p})\mu_0\). Thus \(K\le\left\lceil c^{-1}n^{\alpha_p}\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon)\right\rceil\) accepted iterations suffice. The order \(p\) alone does not determine \(\alpha_p\): a concrete higher-order complexity claim additionally requires a neighborhood invariant, an acceptance rule, and a proved dimension-dependent decrease estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A higher-order model's iteration bound follows from its proved contraction exponent; model order alone does not determine that exponent.
knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Order Iteration Complexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is only a generic contraction template: order p does not determine the exponent, and no concrete higher-order algorithm, invariant, acceptance rule, or source supplies one. It therefore cannot yet serve as a higher-order iteration-complexity record.

children.title: Mehrotra Worst-Case Guarantee Boundary
children.top_down_role: The separation between practical predictor-corrector performance and classical polynomial guarantees.

assumptions_latex: Mehrotra's heuristic chooses centering and step parameters from an affine-scaling prediction.
No uniform invariant is assumed that guarantees neighborhood preservation and a dimension-controlled decrease at every iteration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The classical \(O(\sqrt n\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon))\) path-following guarantee cannot be inferred for the unmodified heuristic from predictor-corrector structure alone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between Mehrotra's practical heuristic and neighborhood-based polynomial predictor-corrector analyses.

source_refs.locator: Mehrotra's Predictor-Corrector Algorithm p. 14
Polynomial Versus Exponential, Worst Case Versus Average Case p. 50

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A predictor-corrector label does not itself imply polynomial complexity. The standard estimate \(K=O(\sqrt n\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon))\) requires a uniform neighborhood invariant and a decrease such as \(\mu_{k+1}\le(1-\delta/\sqrt n)\mu_k\). Mehrotra's unmodified adaptive centering and step choices do not, merely by their definition, supply these two inequalities. Accordingly its strong practical performance is not by itself a classical worst-case polynomial certificate; such a guarantee requires additional safeguards or a separate analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mehrotra's heuristic structure alone does not provide the invariants needed for the classical polynomial path-following bound; safeguards or another proof are required.

children.title: Primal-Dual Approximate Optimality
children.top_down_role: Approximate optimality interfaces combining primal, dual, and gap information.

assumptions_latex: The primal problem is \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) and the dual is \(\max\{b^Ty:A^Ty+s=c,\ s\ge0\}\).
Tolerances \(\varepsilon_p,\varepsilon_d,\varepsilon_g\ge0\) and norms on the residual spaces are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The tuple certifies primal residual at most \(\varepsilon_p\), dual residual at most \(\varepsilon_d\), and normalized duality gap at most \(\varepsilon_g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-and-gap certificate for the standard equality-form primal-dual LP pair.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A tuple \((x,y,s)\) is an \((\varepsilon_p,\varepsilon_d,\varepsilon_g)\)-approximate primal-dual certificate when \(x\ge0\), \(s\ge0\), \(\|Ax-b\|\le\varepsilon_p\), \(\|A^Ty+s-c\|\le\varepsilon_d\), and \(|c^Tx-b^Ty|/(1+|c^Tx|+|b^Ty|)\le\varepsilon_g\). Each displayed quantity is directly computable from the data and tuple. When all tolerances vanish, these conditions reduce to primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and equality of objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative primal-dual tuple certifies approximate optimality by meeting stated primal residual, dual residual, and normalized objective-gap tolerances.

knowledge_statements.title: Scaled Residual Certification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One explicit Euclidean normwise scaling convention for reporting LP residuals and objective gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Using Euclidean vector norms and the spectral matrix norm, define \(\rho_p=\|Ax-b\|_2/(1+\|A\|_2\|x\|_2+\|b\|_2)\), \(\rho_d=\|A^Ty+s-c\|_2/(1+\|A\|_2\|y\|_2+\|s\|_2+\|c\|_2)\), and \(\rho_g=|c^Tx-b^Ty|/(1+|c^Tx|+|b^Ty|)\). The conditions \(x\ge0\), \(s\ge0\), and \(\max\{\rho_p,\rho_d,\rho_g\}\le\varepsilon\) form a directly checkable scale-aware certificate under this declared normalization. Other solver interfaces may use different explicitly reported denominators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Using declared Euclidean and spectral norms, normalize primal residual, dual residual, and objective gap by explicit data-and-iterate scales and compare their maximum with the requested tolerance.
assumptions_latex: The LP data are \((A,b,c)\), and \((x,y,s)\) satisfies \(x\ge0\) and \(s\ge0\).
Euclidean vector norms and the spectral matrix norm are used, and every denominator below is at least one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{\rho_p,\rho_d,\rho_g\}\le\varepsilon\) is a scale-aware, directly checkable approximate-solution certificate under the declared normalization.

children.title: Centrality-Aware Termination
children.top_down_role: Termination interfaces incorporating path proximity as well as residual and gap quality.

assumptions_latex: Tolerances \(\varepsilon_p,\varepsilon_d,\varepsilon_g\ge0\) and a neighborhood radius \(0\le\theta<1\) are prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Residual, gap, and centrality tests jointly certify termination near the primal-dual central path.

source_refs.locator: A Primal-Dual Framework p. 8
Primal-Dual Methods: Development of the Fundamental Ideas p. 43

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A centrality-aware stopping test accepts \((x,y,s)\) when \(\|Ax-b\|\le\varepsilon_p\), \(\|A^Ty+s-c\|\le\varepsilon_d\), \(x^Ts/n\le\varepsilon_g\), and \(\|XSe-\mu e\|_2\le\theta\mu\). The first two inequalities test feasibility, the third tests average complementarity, and the fourth verifies membership in the two-norm centrality neighborhood. Omitting the fourth still permits approximate optimality reporting but no longer certifies proximity to the central path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Terminate only when primal and dual residuals, average complementarity, and distance from uniform complementarity all satisfy their declared tolerances.
knowledge_statements.title: Centrality-Aware Termination

children.title: Primal-Infeasibility Certificates
children.top_down_role: Dual-ray certificate families for primal infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Infeasibility Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Farkas-type dual certificate for equality constraints with nonnegative primal variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal feasibility system \(Ax=b\), \(x\ge0\), any vector \(y\) satisfying \(A^Ty\ge0\) componentwise and \(b^Ty<0\) certifies that the primal system is infeasible. The certificate is checked by evaluating \(A^Ty\) and \(b^Ty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector whose transpose action on A is componentwise nonnegative but whose inner product with b is negative certifies that the primal system has no nonnegative solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The system \(Ax=b\), \(x\ge0\) is infeasible.

source_refs.locator: A Primal-Dual Framework p. 8

source_witnesses.locator: A Primal-Dual Framework p. 8

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Farkas Alternative for Nonnegative Equality Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact theorem of alternatives for equality constraints with componentwise nonnegative primal variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exactly one of the following systems is feasible: \(Ax=b,\ x\ge0\); or \(A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0,\ b^{\mathsf T}y<0\). Equivalently, \(\{x\ge0:Ax=b\}=\varnothing\) if and only if there exists \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) such that \(A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative equality system is infeasible exactly when it has a Farkas multiplier with nonnegative transformed coefficients and strictly negative right-hand-side pairing.
assumptions_latex: The multiplier \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) is unrestricted in sign.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x\ge0:Ax=b\}=\varnothing\iff\exists y\in\mathbb R^m:\ A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0,\ b^{\mathsf T}y<0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Farkas Alternative for Nonnegative Equality Systems

children.title: Dual-Infeasibility Ray Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Primal-ray certificate families associated with dual infeasibility.

children.title: Dual-Infeasibility Rays
children.top_down_role: Ray certificates interpreted through failure of dual feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Infeasibility Rays
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal recession direction as a certificate that the standard-form dual is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the dual feasibility system \(A^Ty+s=c\), \(s\ge0\), a nonzero vector \(d\) satisfying \(Ad=0\), \(d\ge0\), and \(c^Td<0\) is a dual-infeasibility ray. If \(x\) is primal feasible, then \(x+td\) is primal feasible for every \(t\ge0\), and \(c^T(x+td)\to-\infty\) as \(t\to\infty\). Thus the ray also certifies primal unboundedness when primal feasibility is established.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero nonnegative nullspace direction with negative objective slope certifies dual infeasibility and, when a primal feasible point exists, primal unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The dual system is infeasible, and every primal feasible point \(x\) generates the improving ray \(x+td\) for \(t\ge0\).

source_refs.locator: A Primal-Dual Framework p. 8

source_witnesses.locator: A Primal-Dual Framework p. 8

children.title: Primal-Unboundedness Rays
children.top_down_role: Ray certificates interpreted through unbounded primal descent.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Unboundedness Rays
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recession certificate for an equality-form minimization LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the primal problem \(\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\). A vector \(d\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfying \(Ad=0\), \(d\ge0\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\) is a primal-unboundedness ray. If \(x^0\) is primal feasible, then \(x(t)=x^0+td\) is feasible for every \(t\ge0\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}x(t)=c^{\mathsf T}x^0+t c^{\mathsf T}d\to-\infty\). Thus \(d\) verifiably certifies primal unboundedness; moreover, it contradicts feasibility of the dual system \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative null-space direction with negative objective slope certifies unboundedness whenever a primal feasible point exists, and it also proves dual infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n},\ b\in\mathbb R^m,\ c\in\mathbb R^n\).
The primal feasible set is nonempty when primal unboundedness is concluded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ad=0,\ d\ge0,\ c^{\mathsf T}d<0\Longrightarrow \inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}=-\infty\) when the primal is feasible.

source_refs.locator: A Primal-Dual Framework p. 8

source_witnesses.locator: A Primal-Dual Framework p. 8

children.title: Ray-Based Status Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Connections between dual-infeasibility status and primal-unboundedness status.

knowledge_statements.title: Ray-Based Status Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Status implications for recession rays in the standard primal-dual pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal-dual pair \(\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) and \(\sup\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\ge0\}\), existence of \(d\ge0\) with \(Ad=0\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\) implies dual infeasibility. If the primal is also feasible, the same ray implies primal unboundedness. Conversely, if the primal is feasible and has value \(-\infty\), then such a ray exists. Hence a ray alone establishes dual infeasibility, while the status correspondence with primal unboundedness additionally requires primal feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative-cost primal recession ray always proves dual infeasibility and, together with primal feasibility, is equivalent to primal unboundedness.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n},\ b\in\mathbb R^m,\ c\in\mathbb R^n\).
Both programs use the displayed equality-form primal-dual convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists d\ge0:Ad=0,\ c^{\mathsf T}d<0\Rightarrow\) dual infeasibility, and under primal feasibility this is equivalent to primal unboundedness.

source_refs.locator: A Primal-Dual Framework p. 8

source_witnesses.locator: A Primal-Dual Framework p. 8

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure of the converse from dual infeasibility to primal unboundedness when primal feasibility is absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=[0]\), \(b=[1]\), and \(c=[-1]\). Then \(0x=1\) makes the primal infeasible, while \(0\cdot y+s=-1\), \(s\ge0\), makes the dual infeasible. Nevertheless \(d=1\) satisfies \(Ad=0\), \(d\ge0\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}d=-1<0\). Thus a dual-infeasibility ray can exist while the primal is infeasible rather than unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inconsistent one-variable primal with negative cost has a dual-infeasibility ray but no primal-unboundedness status because it has no feasible point.
assumptions_latex: The primal is \(\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), with dual feasibility system \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The dual is infeasible and \(d=1\) is a dual-infeasibility ray, but the primal feasible set is empty and hence the primal is not unbounded below in the status sense requiring feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Infeasibility Without Primal Unboundedness

knowledge_statements.title: Embedded Outcome Classification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification for a homogeneous embedding of an equality-form primal-dual LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a nonzero embedded solution satisfy \(Ax-b\tau=0\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s-c\tau=0\), \(c^{\mathsf T}x-b^{\mathsf T}y+\kappa=0\), and \((x,s,\tau,\kappa)\ge0\). If \(\tau>0\), then \(\kappa=0\) and \((x/\tau,y/\tau,s/\tau)\) is a primal-dual optimal solution. If \(\tau=0\) and \(\kappa>0\), then \(c^{\mathsf T}x-b^{\mathsf T}y<0\); consequently either \(c^{\mathsf T}x<0\) gives a dual-infeasibility ray or \(b^{\mathsf T}y>0\) gives a primal-infeasibility certificate, possibly both.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive embedding scale recovers an optimum; a positive certificate scale yields at least one primal- or dual-infeasibility certificate.
assumptions_latex: The primal is \(\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) and the dual uses \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\ge0\).
The displayed embedded point is nonzero and satisfies all embedding equations exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau>0\) yields primal-dual optimality, whereas \(\tau=0<\kappa\) yields an alternative-system certificate.
review_flags: Exact embedding convention and classification require an authoritative homogeneous-embedding locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The classification is plausible for the displayed homogeneous embedding, but no authoritative source identifies this exact sign convention and outcome theorem. The dimensions and domain of y are also not explicitly introduced. A source specific to this embedding is required before selecting a definitive replacement.

children.title: Missing Strict Interior
children.top_down_role: Instances outside the domain of the ordinary full-dimensional logarithmic barrier.

knowledge_statements.title: Missing Strict Interior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain boundary of the ordinary logarithmic barrier for equality-form LPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), the ordinary barrier subproblem \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x-\mu\sum_{i=1}^n\log x_i:Ax=b\}\) has domain \(P_{++}=\{x:Ax=b,\ x>0\}\). If \(P\ne\varnothing\) but \(P_{++}=\varnothing\), the full-dimensional logarithmic barrier is nowhere finite on the feasible set, so its ordinary central path is undefined. A facial reduction, elimination of variables fixed at zero, or a relative-interior barrier is then required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible LP without a strictly positive feasible point lies outside the domain of the ordinary full-dimensional logarithmic central path.
assumptions_latex: The logarithmic barrier includes every nonnegativity coordinate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\ne\varnothing\) and \(P_{++}=\varnothing\Longrightarrow\) the ordinary logarithmic central path is undefined.

source_refs.source_title: Interior Point Methods for Linear Optimization
source_refs.locator: 5.3 The primal logarithmic barrier function p. 90

source_witnesses.source_title: Interior Point Methods for Linear Optimization
source_witnesses.locator: 5.3 The primal logarithmic barrier function p. 90

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Facial Certificate for Missing Strict Interior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alternative-system certificate exposing coordinates that every feasible point must set to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\ge0:Ax=b\}\ne\varnothing\). Then \(P\cap\mathbb R_{++}^n=\varnothing\) if and only if there exists \(y\) such that \[z=A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0,\qquad z\ne0,\qquad b^{\mathsf T}y=0.\] For every \(x\in P\), \(z^{\mathsf T}x=y^{\mathsf T}b=0\); hence each coordinate satisfying \(z_i>0\) is fixed at zero throughout \(P\). Eliminating exposed coordinates is a valid facial-reduction step before constructing a relative-interior barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty standard-form feasible set lacks a strictly positive point exactly when a nonzero nonnegative row-space vector exposes coordinates forced to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\cap\mathbb R_{++}^n=\varnothing\iff\exists y:\ A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0,\ A^{\mathsf T}y\ne0,\ b^{\mathsf T}y=0\).

notation.meaning: Nonnegative exposing vector in the row space of A.

knowledge_statements.title: Facial Certificate for Missing Strict Interior

children.title: Degenerate Optimal Faces
children.top_down_role: Degenerate or nonunique solution structures affecting path limits and identification.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Optimal Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limit selection by the central path when the optimal set is non-singleton.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the primal LP has a strictly feasible point, a finite optimum, and a bounded nonempty optimal face \(F^*\). For every \(\mu>0\), let \(x(\mu)\) minimize \(c^{\mathsf T}x-\mu\sum_i\log x_i\) over \(Ax=b\) and \(x>0\). As \(\mu\downarrow0\), the path need not identify a unique vertex; instead it converges to the analytic center of the relative interior of \(F^*\) after coordinates identically zero on \(F^*\) are omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With multiple optima, the central path selects the optimal face’s relative analytic center rather than an arbitrary optimal vertex.
assumptions_latex: The primal feasible region has a strictly positive point.
The optimal face is nonempty and bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x(\mu)\to\operatorname{ac}(F^*)\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\), with the analytic center taken relative to \(F^*\).

notation.meaning: relative analytic center of the optimal face
